   1: # Rustynet Phase 1 Implementation (Production-Grade)
   2: 
   3: ## 1) Objective and Exact Phase 1 Boundaries
   4: Phase 1 delivers architecture and security foundations that are mandatory for safe implementation of all later features. Phase 1 is complete only when boundaries, contracts, security baselines, and quality gates are codified and testable.
   5: 
   6: ### In Scope (Phase 1)
   7: - Rust workspace and crate boundary enforcement for:
   8:   - `crates/rustynet-control`
   9:   - `crates/rustynetd`
  10:   - `crates/rustynet-cli`
  11:   - `crates/rustynet-relay`
  12:   - `crates/rustynet-policy`
  13:   - `crates/rustynet-crypto`
  14:   - `crates/rustynet-backend-api`
  15:   - `crates/rustynet-backend-wireguard`
  16: - Protocol-agnostic backend abstraction contract (`TunnelBackend`) with explicit capability model.
  17: - Hard separation rule: no WireGuard-specific types/config semantics in control-plane, policy, or domain crates.
  18: - Security baseline artifacts:
  19:   - key hierarchy and custody model
  20:   - token model and revocation semantics
  21:   - threat model v1 and trust boundaries
  22:   - authentication abuse-control baseline
  23:   - cryptographic allowlist/denylist and deprecation policy
  24: - Engineering quality baseline:
  25:   - CI command gates and failure criteria
  26:   - backend contract test harness skeleton
  27:   - performance harness skeleton and budget definitions
  28: 
  29: ### Out of Scope (Not Phase 1 Delivery)
  30: - Production enrollment/auth endpoint implementation.
  31: - Linux/macOS/Windows production tunnel plumbing.
  32: - Exit node, LAN toggle, Magic DNS runtime behavior.
  33: - Multi-tenant, UI, SSO, compliance operations.
  34: 
  35: These features are intentionally excluded from Phase 1 implementation scope and are addressed by their owning phase documents without changing Phase 1 boundaries.
  36: 
  37: ## 2) Normative References and Precedence Rules
  38: ### Normative References
  39: 1. [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md)
  40: 2. [SecurityMinimumBar.md](./SecurityMinimumBar.md)
  41: 3. [Phase1.md](./Phase1.md)
  42: 4. [Phase2.md](./Phase2.md) through [Phase9.md](./Phase9.md) (forward-compatibility constraints only)
  43: 5. Current workspace architecture:
  44:    - `/Users/iwanteague/Desktop/Rustynet/Cargo.toml`
  45:    - `/Users/iwanteague/Desktop/Rustynet/crates/*`
  46: 
  47: ### Precedence Rules
  48: 1. `Requirements.md` is the source of truth for product/security requirements.
  49: 2. `SecurityMinimumBar.md` is release-blocking and cannot be weakened.
  50: 3. `Phase1.md` defines the required delivery slice for this phase.
  51: 4. This document defines executable implementation details for Phase 1 and cannot contradict items 1-3.
  52: 5. Phase 2-9 documents may influence interface extensibility decisions, but cannot alter Phase 1 requirements.
  53: 
  54: ### Conflict Resolution
  55: - If any implementation detail in this document conflicts with `Requirements.md`, update this document to match requirements immediately.
  56: - If a security control in this document is weaker than `SecurityMinimumBar.md`, the control is invalid and must be replaced with the stronger requirement.
  57: - If code behavior differs from this document, code is treated as non-compliant until corrected.
  58: 
  59: ## 3) Final Architecture for Phase 1 (Crate Ownership and Responsibilities)
  60: ### Workspace Ownership Model
  61: - `rustynet-backend-api`:
  62:   - Owns protocol-agnostic transport domain contract.
  63:   - Owns `TunnelBackend`, `BackendCapabilities`, backend errors, route/peer/runtime types.
  64:   - Must not import any protocol adapter crate.
  65: - `rustynet-backend-wireguard`:
  66:   - Owns WireGuard adapter implementation only.
  67:   - May translate generic backend contract into WireGuard-specific runtime behavior.
  68:   - Must not leak WireGuard-specific types through public API outside adapter crate.
  69: - `rustynetd`:
  70:   - Owns client daemon orchestration.
  71:   - Consumes `TunnelBackend` trait object; does not depend on WireGuard internals.
  72:   - Owns runtime sequencing rules (start/configure/apply_routes/set_exit_mode/shutdown).
  73: - `rustynet-control`:
  74:   - Owns control-plane architecture baseline, signing-policy baseline, and policy decision integration contract.
  75:   - Must remain protocol-agnostic.
  76: - `rustynet-policy`:
  77:   - Owns default-deny policy primitives and deterministic evaluation rules.
  78:   - Must not know tunnel/backend internals.
  79: - `rustynet-crypto`:
  80:   - Owns crypto material handling primitives, key hierarchy model, algorithm policy enforcement.
  81:   - Owns secure-memory handling requirements (zeroization) and key-custody interface baseline.
  82: - `rustynet-cli`:
  83:   - Owns operator/user command interface surface.
  84:   - Must call daemon/control contracts; no backend-specific assumptions.
  85: - `rustynet-relay`:
  86:   - Owns ciphertext-forwarding service boundary definition only.
  87:   - Must never require payload decryption capability.
  88: 
  89: ### Enforced Dependency Direction
  90: - Allowed:
  91:   - `rustynetd -> rustynet-backend-api`, `rustynetd -> rustynet-policy`, `rustynetd -> rustynet-crypto`
  92:   - `rustynet-backend-wireguard -> rustynet-backend-api`
  93:   - `rustynet-control -> rustynet-policy`, `rustynet-control -> rustynet-crypto`
  94: - Disallowed:
  95:   - `rustynet-control -> rustynet-backend-wireguard`
  96:   - `rustynet-policy -> rustynet-backend-wireguard`
  97:   - `rustynet-backend-api -> rustynet-backend-wireguard`
  98:   - Any crate importing WireGuard-specific symbols except `rustynet-backend-wireguard`
  99: 
 100: ### Architectural Guardrails
 101: - Rust-first implementation across all core components.
 102: - `unsafe` remains forbidden at workspace level.
 103: - Control/policy/domain models remain transport-protocol-agnostic.
 104: - Adapter-specific behavior is isolated to adapter crate(s).
 105: 
 106: ## 4) Backend Abstraction Contract Details (TunnelBackend Boundary, Capabilities, Invariants)
 107: ### Contract Surface (Phase 1 Baseline)
 108: `TunnelBackend` methods are the only allowed control point for data-plane orchestration in Phase 1:
 109: - `name()`
 110: - `capabilities()`
 111: - `start(context)`
 112: - `configure_peer(peer)`
 113: - `remove_peer(node_id)`
 114: - `apply_routes(routes)`
 115: - `set_exit_mode(mode)`
 116: - `stats()`
 117: - `shutdown()`
 118: 
 119: ### Capability Contract
 120: `BackendCapabilities` is authoritative for feature checks:
 121: - `supports_roaming`
 122: - `supports_exit_nodes`
 123: - `supports_lan_routes`
 124: - `supports_ipv6`
 125: 
 126: Fail-closed rule: unsupported capability requests must return an error and must not silently degrade behavior.
 127: 
 128: ### Invariants
 129: 1. `start` may be called only once per running lifecycle; second call must fail.
 130: 2. `configure_peer`, `remove_peer`, `apply_routes`, `set_exit_mode`, and `stats` require running state.
 131: 3. `shutdown` clears in-memory peer/route/session state and resets exit mode.
 132: 4. `NodeId` and peer identifiers must be non-empty and canonicalized before insertion.
 133: 5. `apply_routes` is replace-all semantics for deterministic route state.
 134: 6. Backend errors must be typed (`InvalidInput`, `AlreadyRunning`, `NotRunning`, `Internal`) and non-ambiguous.
 135: 7. No method may expose protocol-specific internal representations to callers.
 136: 
 137: ### Boundary Enforcement
 138: - Enforcement point:
 139:   - `crates/rustynet-backend-api/src/lib.rs` type system and public API boundary.
 140:   - crate import policies in workspace review/CI checks.
 141: - Verification method:
 142:   - compile-time dependency checks.
 143:   - grep-based boundary tests for protocol symbol leakage.
 144:   - backend contract tests validating lifecycle/error invariants.
 145: 
 146: ## 5) Security Baseline Implementation
 147: ### 5.1 Threat Model v1
 148: ### Assets
 149: - Node private identity keys.
 150: - Control-plane signing keys and trust state.
 151: - Enrollment/auth tokens and one-time credentials.
 152: - Policy definitions and route authority data.
 153: - Audit trail integrity.
 154: 
 155: ### Adversaries
 156: - Internet attacker performing brute-force, replay, and abuse traffic.
 157: - Malicious insider or compromised admin endpoint.
 158: - Compromised node attempting lateral movement or privilege escalation.
 159: - Attacker with temporary access to disk backups or host filesystem.
 160: - Adversary attempting protocol confusion or weak-algorithm downgrade.
 161: 
 162: ### Security Objectives
 163: - Preserve confidentiality/integrity of mesh and control-plane operations.
 164: - Enforce default-deny authorization and route policy.
 165: - Prevent replay and abuse-driven state exhaustion.
 166: - Prevent key/token leakage from logs/config surfaces.
 167: - Preserve protocol modularity without reducing security controls.
 168: 
 169: ### 5.2 Trust Boundaries
 170: 1. Client daemon (`rustynetd`) boundary:
 171: - Crossing data: policy snapshots, peer maps, tokens, runtime commands.
 172: - Enforcement: signature verification requirement, strict schema validation, redaction-safe logging.
 173: 
 174: 2. Control-plane boundary (`rustynet-control`):
 175: - Crossing data: enrollment/auth requests, node metadata mutations.
 176: - Enforcement: TLS 1.3 only, abuse controls (rate limit/lockout/replay), RBAC baseline contract.
 177: 
 178: 3. Backend boundary (`rustynet-backend-api` to adapter):
 179: - Crossing data: generic peer/route/runtime instructions.
 180: - Enforcement: trait invariants, capability checks, typed errors, no protocol leakage.
 181: 
 182: 4. Key custody boundary (`rustynet-crypto` to OS/file system):
 183: - Crossing data: encrypted key blobs, key metadata, memory-resident secrets.
 184: - Enforcement: secure storage selection, permission checks, zeroization, fail-closed startup.
 185: 
 186: ### 5.3 Auth Attack-Surface Controls (Baseline Spec)
 187: These controls are mandatory Phase 1 baseline definitions and must be implemented through shared middleware contracts in Phase 2 without changing defaults.
 188: 
 189: 1. Rate limiting:
 190: - Default: per-IP token bucket (burst 20, refill 10/min), per-identity (burst 10, refill 5/15min).
 191: - Enforcement point: `rustynet-control` auth middleware interface.
 192: - Verification: negative tests must prove throttling under burst traffic.
 193: 
 194: 2. Lockout/backoff:
 195: - Default: exponential backoff starting at 30s, capped at 15m, reset only after successful auth + cooldown.
 196: - Enforcement point: auth decision engine contract in `rustynet-control`.
 197: - Verification: deterministic test cases for repeated failures and cooldown reset.
 198: 
 199: 3. Anti-replay:
 200: - Default token lifetime: 5 minutes; nonce/state required for all state-changing auth/enrollment operations.
 201: - Clock skew tolerance: +/- 90 seconds; beyond this => reject.
 202: - Enforcement point: token validation and nonce store interface.
 203: - Verification: replay token reuse tests, stale token tests, skew boundary tests.
 204: 
 205: 4. Abuse visibility:
 206: - Baseline signal fields: source IP, identity handle, endpoint, failure class, limiter decision.
 207: - Enforcement point: structured security event schema in `rustynet-control`.
 208: - Verification: test asserts required fields exist and secrets are redacted.
 209: 
 210: Fail-closed rule: if abuse-control subsystem state cannot be read or updated, auth/enrollment operation is denied.
 211: 
 212: ### 5.4 Key Custody Fallback Behavior
 213: 1. Primary storage:
 214: - OS secure key storage APIs when available.
 215: 
 216: 2. Fallback storage (when OS key store unavailable):
 217: - Encrypted-at-rest key blob using AEAD (`AES-256-GCM` or `XChaCha20-Poly1305` via vetted library).
 218: - Envelope key derived with `Argon2id` from operator-provided secret plus per-host salt.
 219: - File permissions enforced at startup (`0700` directory, `0600` file, owner-only access).
 220: - Automatic startup refusal on permission mismatch or encryption metadata mismatch.
 221: 
 222: 3. Memory handling:
 223: - Sensitive key material wrapped in zeroizing containers (`zeroize` semantics).
 224: - Debug and log formatting for secret types must redact bytes by default.
 225: 
 226: 4. Trust-state persistence:
 227: - Signed-authorization trust state must be integrity-checked on load.
 228: - Missing/corrupt/unwritable trust state => trust-required operations denied with explicit operator error.
 229: 
 230: Verification methods:
 231: - permission-check unit/integration tests.
 232: - corrupted-keystore negative tests.
 233: - trust-state unavailable tests asserting fail-closed behavior.
 234: - memory redaction tests for debug/log code paths.
 235: 
 236: ### 5.5 Cryptographic Allowlist/Denylist and Deprecation Policy
 237: ### Allowlist (Phase 1 Baseline)
 238: - Transport security:
 239:   - TLS 1.3 only (`rustls`) for control-plane transport.
 240:   - WireGuard protocol model for tunnel crypto (no custom protocol).
 241: - Signatures:
 242:   - `Ed25519` for control-plane signed artifacts.
 243: - Hash/KDF:
 244:   - `SHA-256`/`SHA-512`, `BLAKE2s/BLAKE2b` where applicable.
 245:   - `HKDF-SHA256` and `Argon2id` for approved derivation contexts.
 246: - AEAD (non-tunnel local storage contexts):
 247:   - `AES-256-GCM` or `XChaCha20-Poly1305`.
 248: 
 249: ### Denylist (Hard Rejection)
 250: - `MD5`, `SHA-1` for security integrity/signing.
 251: - `RC4`, `DES`, `3DES`, `BF-CBC`, and non-AEAD CBC tunnel/storage modes.
 252: - Static/shared long-lived session keys without rekey model.
 253: - Weak DH groups (< 2048-bit) and protocol downgrade paths.
 254: 
 255: ### Deprecation and Exception Policy
 256: - Insecure compatibility modes default to disabled.
 257: - Any temporary exception requires:
 258:   - documented risk owner
 259:   - explicit expiry date
 260:   - runtime auto-expiry behavior
 261:   - explicit operator-visible warning
 262: - After expiry, system returns to deny mode automatically.
 263: 
 264: Enforcement point:
 265: - `rustynet-crypto` algorithm policy module and config validation at startup.
 266: 
 267: Verification:
 268: - allowlist/denylist unit tests.
 269: - configuration negative tests that must fail startup on denied algorithm.
 270: - test that expired exception entries are rejected.
 271: 
 272: ## 6) Data Model and State Strategy for Phase 1
 273: ### Phase 1 Canonical Domain Types
 274: - Backend domain (`rustynet-backend-api`):
 275:   - `NodeId`
 276:   - `SocketEndpoint`
 277:   - `PeerConfig`
 278:   - `Route` + `RouteKind`
 279:   - `RuntimeContext`
 280:   - `BackendCapabilities`
 281:   - `TunnelStats`
 282:   - `BackendError` + `BackendErrorKind`
 283: - Policy domain (`rustynet-policy`):
 284:   - `PolicyRule`
 285:   - `AccessRequest`
 286:   - `Decision`
 287: - Crypto domain (`rustynet-crypto`):
 288:   - `PublicKey`
 289:   - `SecretKey`
 290:   - `NodeKeyPair`
 291:   - `CryptoError`
 292: 
 293: ### State Strategy
 294: 1. Runtime state:
 295: - Backend lifecycle state in-memory only (`not running` or `running`).
 296: - Peer/route state maintained by backend adapter with deterministic replace/clear semantics.
 297: 
 298: 2. Security policy state:
 299: - Cryptographic allowlist/denylist and abuse-control defaults are versioned configuration artifacts.
 300: - Any invalid security policy load results in startup failure (fail-closed).
 301: 
 302: 3. Trust and key state:
 303: - Trust-required state cannot be treated as optional.
 304: - Key custody must pass secure-store or encrypted-fallback checks before service start.
 305: 
 306: 4. Schema/version strategy:
 307: - All security-relevant config structures include explicit version field (`v1` baseline).
 308: - Unknown major versions are rejected at load time.
 309:

 459: ## 11) Risks and Mitigations for Phase 1 (Including Explicit Fail-Closed Decisions)
 460: | Risk | Impact | Mitigation | Fail-Closed Decision | Verification |
 461: |---|---|---|---|---|
 462: | Protocol leakage from adapter into core domain | Breaks backend modularity; blocks future backend replacement | Enforce crate boundaries and leakage CI gate | Any leakage match blocks merge | Section 7.7 gate |
 463: | Weak/legacy crypto enabled by config drift | Confidentiality/integrity regression | Allowlist/denylist enforcement at startup | Invalid/weak algorithm config aborts startup | Crypto policy tests |
 464: | Key store unavailable or insecure permissions | Private key compromise risk | OS keystore-first and encrypted fallback with strict perms | If neither secure path available, daemon/control refuses to start | Permission/corruption tests |
 465: | Abuse-control subsystem unavailable | Brute-force/replay exposure | Baseline middleware contract requires limiter + nonce state checks | Auth/enrollment request denied when control state unavailable | Negative integration tests |
 466: | Trust/signing state missing or corrupt | Unauthorized peer-map/state acceptance risk | Integrity checks before trust-required operations | Trust-required operations blocked with explicit operator error | Trust-state load tests |
 467: | Secret leakage in logs/debug output | Credential compromise | Redacted secret wrappers and log policy tests | Any secret redaction failure fails CI and blocks merge | Redaction tests + gate |
 468: | CI dependency-vuln gate bypass | Known vulnerable dependency shipped | Mandatory `cargo audit` + `cargo deny` gates | Merge blocked on unresolved critical/high findings | CI gate enforcement |
 469: | Performance harness schema drift | Missing regression signal | Fixed JSON schema with mandatory keys/reason codes | Missing key/invalid reason code fails CI | Perf harness validator |

===== /documents/Phase2.md =====

   1: # Rustynet Phase 2 Plan (Identity, Enrollment, and Control-Plane Core)
   2: 
   3: ## 0) Document Relationship and Scope
   4: - This plan extends architecture outputs from [Phase1.md](./Phase1.md).
   5: - Requirement ownership remains in [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md).
   6: - Phase 2 outputs are prerequisites for [Phase3.md](./Phase3.md).
   7: - If this plan conflicts with [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md), requirements take precedence.
   8: 
   9: ## 1) Phase 2 Objective
  10: Deliver secure identity and enrollment flows with auditable control-plane APIs, without yet taking on full data-plane feature scope.
  11: 
  12: ## 2) Phase 2 Scope
  13: 1. Identity and auth core:
  14: - User auth baseline (local auth first, extensible for OIDC later).
  15: - Device/node identity key registration.
  16: - Short-lived access tokens and refresh/renew patterns.
  17: 
  18: 2. Throwaway credential lifecycle:
  19: - Implement one-time credential states: `created`, `used`, `expired`, `revoked`.
  20: - Enforce `max_uses = 1` with immediate invalidation after first successful use.
  21: - Enforce atomic consume semantics using write-time revalidation in a single transaction.
  22: - Add uniqueness constraints preventing key reuse under concurrent consume attempts.
  23: - Add audit events for every lifecycle transition.
  24: 
  25: 3. Control-plane API core:
  26: - Enrollment endpoints.
  27: - Node registration and metadata update endpoints.
  28: - Signed peer-map delivery mechanism.
  29: - Policy-fetch endpoint scaffolding.
  30: 
  31: 4. Persistence baseline:
  32: - Persist users, nodes, credentials, and lifecycle events.
  33: - SQLite-first schema designed for later Postgres migration.
  34: 
  35: 5. Trust-state persistence baseline:
  36: - Persist trusted authorization/signing state with integrity checks.
  37: - If trusted state is missing/corrupt/unwritable, trust-required operations must fail closed.
  38: 
  39: 6. Authentication and API abuse hardening:
  40: - Enforce per-IP and per-identity rate limiting for auth/enrollment endpoints.
  41: - Enforce lockout/backoff controls for repeated failures.
  42: - Enforce anti-replay controls (nonce/state checks and bounded token lifetimes).
  43: - Add API abuse detection signals and operator alerts.
  44: 
  45: 7. Endpoint key custody baseline:
  46: - Use OS key store where available.
  47: - If unavailable, enforce encrypted-at-rest fallback with strict permissions and startup permission validation.
  48: - Ensure in-memory secret zeroization strategy is implemented for sensitive materials.
  49: 
  50: 8. Credential lifecycle hardening:
  51: - Make one-time enrollment credentials the default.
  52: - Restrict reusable enrollment credentials to automation workflows with short expiry and strict scopes.
  53: - Require secure storage policy for reusable credentials (vault/secret manager; no plaintext distribution).
  54: - Enforce rapid revocation propagation for compromised credentials.
  55: 
  56: ## 3) Deliverables
  57: - Working enrollment flow through CLI + control-plane APIs.
  58: - Throwaway credential generation and lifecycle enforcement.
  59: - Signed peer-map distribution path in place.
  60: - Audit log entries for auth and enrollment actions.
  61: - Reusable credential safety controls and policy enforcement documented and tested.
  62: 
  63: ## 4) Security Gates
  64: - TLS 1.3 enforced on control-plane endpoints.
  65: - Token and credential secrets are never logged.
  66: - Revocation and offboarding path tested for correctness.
  67: - Rate-limit, lockout/backoff, and replay-protection controls are verified with negative tests.
  68: - Auth/enrollment endpoints enforce abuse controls without bypass paths.
  69: - Endpoint key storage fallback passes permission and encryption checks.
  70: - Reusable-credential constraints (scope, expiry, storage policy) are enforced and test-verified.
  71: - Concurrent one-time-key consume tests prove no double-consume behavior.
  72: - Trust-state corruption/unavailability tests prove fail-closed behavior for trust-required operations.
  73: 
  74: ## 5) Phase 2 Exit Criteria
  75: - Normal enrollment and one-time throwaway enrollment both succeed.
  76: - Revoked/expired credentials are rejected deterministically.
  77: - Signed peer maps are validated by clients.
  78: - API and data models remain protocol-agnostic.
  79: - Replay, brute-force, and high-rate abuse test cases are blocked as designed.
  80: - TOCTOU race tests for one-time credentials are passing in CI.
  81: 
  82: ## 6) Handoff to Phase 3
  83: - Phase 3 implements Linux data-plane connectivity using the Phase 1 backend boundary and Phase 2 identity/control artifacts.
  84: - Any data-plane design that leaks WireGuard specifics into control APIs must be rejected.
  85: - Use [Phase3.md](./Phase3.md) as the next execution plan once Phase 2 exit criteria are met.

   1: # Rustynet Phase 3 Plan (Linux Data Plane MVP and Backend Conformance)
   2: 
   3: ## 0) Document Relationship and Scope
   4: - This plan extends identity/control outputs from [Phase2.md](./Phase2.md).
   5: - Requirement ownership remains in [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md).
   6: - Phase 3 outputs are prerequisites for [Phase4.md](./Phase4.md).
   7: - If this plan conflicts with [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md), requirements take precedence.
   8: 
   9: ## 1) Phase 3 Objective
  10: Deliver secure Linux mesh connectivity using a modular WireGuard backend implementation with conformance checks.
  11: 
  12: ## 2) Phase 3 Scope
  13: 1. Linux client daemon core (`rustynetd`):
  14: - TUN lifecycle management.
  15: - Route programming basics.
  16: - Peer session orchestration.
  17: 
  18: 2. WireGuard backend adapter:
  19: - Implement `rustynet-backend-wireguard` against `rustynet-backend-api`.
  20: - Keep WireGuard-specific logic isolated to adapter crate.
  21: 
  22: 3. Connectivity baseline:
  23: - Encrypted node-to-node connectivity for at least 3 nodes.
  24: - Direct path preference with basic relay fallback behavior.
  25: - Session stability across reconnect scenarios.
  26: - Initial performance baseline measurement against declared budgets.
  27: 
  28: 4. Policy enforcement baseline:
  29: - Default-deny behavior active.
  30: - Core allow/deny enforcement in data path.
  31: 
  32: 5. Backend conformance suite v1:
  33: - Define and run tests every backend must pass.
  34: - Include connect/disconnect, peer update, route apply, and teardown behaviors.
  35: 
  36: 6. Handshake and data-plane resilience hardening:
  37: - Add early-drop protections against unauthenticated flood/state exhaustion (for example cookie/challenge or equivalent stateless guard).
  38: - Add handshake path rate controls and adversarial load tests.
  39: - Define and test key rotation/rekey behavior to preserve forward secrecy over long-running sessions.
  40: 
  41: ## 3) Deliverables
  42: - Linux mesh connectivity functioning end-to-end.
  43: - WireGuard adapter passing backend conformance v1.
  44: - Policy enforcement active for baseline mesh flows.
  45: - CI integration tests for 3-node mesh scenarios.
  46: - Performance benchmark report (CPU, memory, reconnect, route-apply latency).
  47: - Handshake-flood resilience test report and mitigations in place.
  48: 
  49: ## 4) Security Gates
  50: - All mesh payload traffic encrypted.
  51: - Client validates signed control-plane data before applying peer updates.
  52: - No leakage of WireGuard types into control-plane API or policy domain.
  53: - Handshake exhaustion and flood tests demonstrate bounded resource impact.
  54: 
  55: ## 5) Phase 3 Exit Criteria
  56: - Three-node Linux mesh passes integration tests consistently.
  57: - Relay fallback functions when direct path is unavailable.
  58: - Backend conformance suite is green for WireGuard adapter.
  59: - Architectural boundary checks confirm protocol-agnostic core model.
  60: - Initial performance budgets are measured and no critical regressions are open.
  61: 
  62: ## 6) Handoff to Phase 4
  63: - Phase 4 adds user-facing networking features (exit node, LAN toggle, Magic DNS) on top of a proven Linux mesh base.
  64: - Use [Phase4.md](./Phase4.md) as the next execution plan once Phase 3 exit criteria are met.

   1: # Rustynet Phase 4 Plan (Exit Nodes, LAN Toggle, and Magic DNS)
   2: 
   3: ## 0) Document Relationship and Scope
   4: - This plan extends mesh baseline outputs from [Phase3.md](./Phase3.md).
   5: - Requirement ownership remains in [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md).
   6: - Phase 4 outputs are prerequisites for [Phase5.md](./Phase5.md).
   7: - If this plan conflicts with [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md), requirements take precedence.
   8: 
   9: ## 1) Phase 4 Objective
  10: Deliver core end-user network features: exit-node routing, LAN access toggling, and Magic DNS.
  11: 
  12: ## 2) Phase 4 Scope
  13: 1. Exit-node feature set:
  14: - Node capability to act as exit node.
  15: - Client-side exit-node selection and disable flows.
  16: - Policy controls for allowed users/groups.
  17: 
  18: 2. LAN access toggle:
  19: - Per-client on/off toggle for exit-node LAN subnets.
  20: - Explicit route advertisement and ACL-gated LAN route access.
  21: - Enforced behavior difference between internet-only and LAN-enabled modes.
  22: - Tunnel and DNS fail-close behavior design for protected-routing modes.
  23: 
  24: 3. Magic DNS baseline:
  25: - Internal DNS naming for nodes.
  26: - Deterministic duplicate-name conflict handling.
  27: - CLI DNS inspection and troubleshooting commands.
  28: 
  29: 4. CLI completion for core networking flows:
  30: - `exit-node select/off`, `lan-access on/off`, `dns inspect`.
  31: 
  32: 5. Leak-class mitigation program:
  33: - Implement route and DNS leak mitigations informed by known VPN leak classes (for example local-network and server-IP leak paths).
  34: - Define OS-specific leak test matrix, starting with Linux and planned parity gates for macOS/Windows.
  35: - Include protocol-filter correctness matrix for shared subnet-router and shared-exit configurations.
  36: 
  37: ## 3) Deliverables
  38: - Exit-node end-to-end traffic routing.
  39: - LAN toggle behavior enforced by policy and routing controls.
  40: - Magic DNS resolution for online nodes.
  41: - Integration tests validating exit + LAN + DNS behavior.
  42: - Leak-class test suite and mitigation matrix for current platform support.
  43: 
  44: ## 4) Security Gates
  45: - LAN routes are never exposed unless explicitly enabled and authorized.
  46: - Default deny remains active for route and peer access.
  47: - DNS record updates require authenticated, authorized control-plane actions.
  48: - Tunnel drop events in protected modes do not leak traffic outside policy (kill-switch behavior).
  49: - Protected DNS modes do not leak DNS requests outside Rustynet policy.
  50: - Protocol-specific ACL intent is preserved for shared-router/shared-exit traffic and never widened during policy transformation.
  51: 
  52: ## 5) Phase 4 Exit Criteria
  53: - Exit-node selection works and can be reverted without stale routes.
  54: - LAN-off mode blocks RFC1918 access through exit node.
  55: - LAN-on mode allows only authorized subnets.
  56: - Magic DNS reliability and naming rules pass integration tests.
  57: - Leak-prevention tests pass for tunnel-failure and DNS-failure scenarios.
  58: - Shared-router/shared-exit protocol-filter test matrix passes without regressions.
  59: 
  60: ## 6) Handoff to Phase 5
  61: - Phase 5 focuses on observability, diagnostics, and reliability hardening of Phase 4 functionality.
  62: - Use [Phase5.md](./Phase5.md) as the next execution plan once Phase 4 exit criteria are met.

   1: # Rustynet Phase 5 Plan (Observability and Reliability Hardening)
   2: 
   3: ## 0) Document Relationship and Scope
   4: - This plan extends networking feature outputs from [Phase4.md](./Phase4.md).
   5: - Requirement ownership remains in [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md).
   6: - Phase 5 outputs are prerequisites for [Phase6.md](./Phase6.md).
   7: - If this plan conflicts with [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md), requirements take precedence.
   8: 
   9: ## 1) Phase 5 Objective
  10: Harden runtime reliability and operational visibility so the platform can be operated safely at small production scale.
  11: 
  12: ## 2) Phase 5 Scope
  13: 1. Observability foundation:
  14: - Structured logs with redaction rules.
  15: - Metrics for control, relay, and client health.
  16: - Health endpoints and status views.
  17: - Tamper-evident, append-only audit log pipeline with integrity verification.
  18: 
  19: 2. Diagnostics tooling:
  20: - `netcheck`/connectivity diagnostics.
  21: - Route and DNS diagnostics.
  22: - Exit-node path visibility (direct vs relay).
  23: 
  24: 3. Reliability hardening:
  25: - Better reconnect and retry behaviors.
  26: - Session persistence behavior across control-plane restarts.
  27: - Backup/restore procedure for control-plane state.
  28: 
  29: 4. Relay hardening:
  30: - Stability improvements for fallback transport.
  31: - Relay health checks and failover behavior.
  32: 
  33: 5. Early release integrity baseline:
  34: - SBOM generation for build artifacts.
  35: - Artifact signing and provenance capture in CI for internal and beta releases.
  36: 
  37: 6. Performance regression guardrails:
  38: - Automated benchmark runs in CI for CPU, memory, reconnect, and route-apply latency.
  39: - Regression thresholds and alerting for performance drift.
  40: 
  41: 7. Vulnerability response operations:
  42: - Define security advisory intake, triage, and disclosure workflow.
  43: - Define patch SLAs by severity and emergency patch release process.
  44: - Define staged release tracks (unstable/canary/stable) for security-sensitive changes.
  45: - Minimum patch SLAs:
  46: - Critical: mitigation or patched build within 48 hours.
  47: - High: patched build within 7 calendar days.
  48: - Medium: patched build within 30 calendar days.
  49: 
  50: 8. Policy safety validation:
  51: - Require policy/ACL validation tests in CI before merge and before rollout.
  52: - Require staged policy rollout with rollback path.
  53: 
  54: 9. Secret redaction assurance:
  55: - Validate secret redaction coverage across MDM, env vars, CLI args, API payloads, and UI-form inputs.
  56: - Add negative tests to ensure no credential/token leakage in normal and error logging paths.
  57: 
  58: ## 3) Deliverables
  59: - Metrics and logs available for all critical components.
  60: - Diagnostics commands usable by operators.
  61: - Reliability tests for reconnect/restart/fallback scenarios.
  62: - Initial runbook set for common operational incidents.
  63: - Tamper-evident audit storage and integrity-check tooling.
  64: - Signed beta artifacts plus SBOM outputs.
  65: - Performance regression dashboard and alerts.
  66: - Security advisory and emergency patch runbooks.
  67: - Policy validation and rollout guardrail tooling.
  68: - Secret-redaction coverage report across all ingestion paths.
  69: 
  70: ## 4) Security Gates
  71: - Logging pipeline verified to avoid credential/token leakage.
  72: - Audit events preserved for operationally sensitive actions.
  73: - Restore procedure validated with integrity checks.
  74: - Audit log integrity checks are automated and detect tampering.
  75: - Build/release pipeline produces signed artifacts and SBOM before distribution.
  76: - Vulnerability response SLAs and emergency patch path are test-exercised.
  77: - Policy changes cannot bypass CI validation and staged rollout controls.
  78: - Critical/high/medium patch SLA compliance is measurable and reported.
  79: - Secret-redaction tests for all ingestion paths are green before release.
  80: 
  81: ## 5) Phase 5 Exit Criteria
  82: - Operators can diagnose major mesh/exit/DNS failures from tooling.
  83: - Recovery from control-plane restart is reliable and tested.
  84: - Relay fallback and recovery are validated under fault scenarios.
  85: - Backup and restore workflow is documented and tested.
  86: - Audit forensics pipeline is operational and tamper-evident.
  87: - Performance regressions are gated by defined thresholds.
  88: - Security operations can produce SLA compliance evidence for advisories and fixes.
  89: 
  90: ## 6) Handoff to Phase 6
  91: - Phase 6 expands user/admin surface and platform support using hardened operational foundations.
  92: - Use [Phase6.md](./Phase6.md) as the next execution plan once Phase 5 exit criteria are met.

  11:

  13: 1. Web admin UI v1:
  14: - Node inventory and state visibility.
  15: - Policy management workflows.
  16: - Exit-node and route control workflows.
  17: - Throwaway credential lifecycle management.
  18: 
  19: 2. Multi-user workflows:
  20: - User and group administration.
  21: - Access review and ownership boundaries.
  22: - Baseline role-based access control (RBAC) for all admin actions.
  23: - Baseline MFA enforcement for privileged admin operations.
  24: - Safe-by-default policy bootstrap to avoid implicit allow-all behavior.
  25:

  27: - macOS client beta quality.
  28: - Windows client beta quality.
  29: - Platform-specific route/firewall/DNS integration hardening.
  30: - Cross-platform leak-class mitigation parity with Linux baseline.
  31: - Privileged helper hardening: argv-only command invocation, strict input validation, and least-privilege execution model.
  32: - Startup wizard host-profile enforcement: detect OS at launch, block unsupported dataplane/runtime operations, and enforce platform-safe storage roots.
  33: 
  34: 4. Packaging and updates:
  35: - Installer strategy and versioning basics.
  36: - Upgrade safety checks.
  37: - Signed artifacts and SBOM are mandatory for beta distribution.
  38:

  41: - Multi-user management workflows functioning.
  42: - macOS and Windows beta clients validated for core use cases.
  43: - Packaging and update flow documentation.
  44: - Policy bootstrap guardrails and unsafe-policy warnings in UI/API flows.
  45: 
  46: ## 4) Security Gates
  47: - Admin operations require authenticated, authorized access.
  48: - Privileged UI actions generate auditable events.
  49: - Platform clients meet same crypto and policy enforcement requirements as Linux.
  50: - RBAC is enforced for admin routes and APIs with deny-by-default behavior.
  51: - MFA is required for privileged mutations (policy, credential, and exit-node administration).
  52: - Admin UI and APIs enforce CSRF protections, secure session/cookie policy, and anti-clickjacking controls.
  53: - Default policy posture cannot silently become allow-all in new deployments.
  54: - macOS/Windows pass leak-class tests required by Phase 4 mitigation matrix.
  55: - Privileged helper paths prove no shell-command construction with untrusted values.
  56: - Host-profile/path-policy checks ensure Linux runtime roots are not used on non-Linux hosts.
  57: 
  58: ## 5) Phase 6 Exit Criteria
  59: - Admins can manage nodes, policies, and credentials via UI.
  60: - macOS and Windows clients complete enrollment and core mesh connectivity reliably.
  61: - Cross-platform policy and exit-node behavior are consistent with Linux baseline.
  62: - RBAC/MFA and web-surface protections pass security tests.
  63: 
  64: ## 6) Handoff to Phase 7
  65: - Phase 7 scales infrastructure and commercial controls after cross-platform and admin UX stabilization.
  66: - Use [Phase7.md](./Phase7.md) as the next execution plan once Phase 6 exit criteria are met.

   1: # Rustynet Phase 7 Plan (Scale and Commercial Foundation)
   2: 
   3: ## 0) Document Relationship and Scope
   4: - This plan extends product expansion outputs from [Phase6.md](./Phase6.md).

   9: ## 1) Phase 7 Objective
  10: Scale the platform architecture and add commercial control primitives for broader customer readiness.
  11: 
  12: ## 2) Phase 7 Scope
  13: 1. Control-plane high availability:
  14: - Postgres-backed persistence for production.
  15: - Stateless API replicas and failover behavior.
  16: - Migration and rollback discipline.
  17: 
  18: 2. Relay fleet maturity:
  19: - Multi-relay deployment support.
  20: - Health-based relay selection.
  21: - Regional relay options.
  22: - Authenticated relay transport behavior that forwards ciphertext only.
  23: - Traversal coordination support for signed endpoint-hint distribution and freshness windows.
  24: - Relay abuse controls (rate limits/quotas) validated under churn and failover.
  25: 
  26: 3. Commercial controls:
  27: - Multi-tenant organization model.
  28: - Plan/feature gating primitives.
  29: - Tenant-level policy boundaries and delegated administration.
  30: 
  31: 4. Enterprise auth baseline:
  32: - OIDC/SSO support.
  33: - Enterprise MFA policy integration and step-up auth compatibility.
  34: 
  35: 5. Control-plane trust hardening mode:
  36: - Add optional coordination-compromise-resilient key authorization mode (tailnet-lock-style trust model).
  37: - Require trusted key set for node-key authorization and auditable key-authority changes.
  38: - Define and test break-glass/disable procedure with explicit secret/material requirements.
  39: - Require trusted-state persistence and integrity checks for trust-hardening mode.
  40: - If trusted state is unavailable/corrupt, trust-hardening mode must fail closed with explicit operator-visible erroring.
  41: 
  42: ## 3) Deliverables
  43: - HA control-plane deployment reference.
  44: - Multi-relay control and health behavior in staging.
  45: - Traversal-aware relay coordination baseline in staging (signed endpoint-hint path).
  46: - Tenant controls and delegated admin boundaries implemented.
  47: - SSO/MFA integration available for production use.
  48: - Control-plane trust-hardening mode available and documented.
  49: 
  50: ## 4) Security Gates
  51: - Tenant-boundary isolation tests pass.
  52: - Privileged operations enforce MFA and auditable authorization.
  53: - HA failover does not bypass policy or revocation controls.
  54: - Trust-hardening mode cannot be bypassed by compromised coordination service alone.
  55: - Trust-hardening mode refuses to operate when trusted state cannot be safely loaded or persisted.
  56: - Relay transport path is ciphertext-only and cannot inspect/decrypt payload content.
  57: - Traversal endpoint-hint replay/tamper checks are enforced and test-backed.
  58: 
  59: ## 5) Phase 7 Exit Criteria
  60: - Platform remains available through tested failover scenarios.
  61: - Multi-tenant boundaries are validated.
  62: - Commercial account controls function with auditable changes.
  63: - Relay fleet behavior is stable under regional/node-level faults and hard-NAT traversal scenarios.
  64: 
  65: ## 6) Handoff to Phase 8
  66: - Phase 8 adds advanced assurance, compliance maturity, and stronger key custody controls.
  67: - Use [Phase8.md](./Phase8.md) as the next execution plan once Phase 7 exit criteria are met.

===== /documents/Requirements.md =====

   1: # Rustynet Requirements (Brainstorm v0.3)
   2: 
   3: ## 0) Document Map and Governance
   4: - This file is the normative source of truth for product requirements across all phases.
   5: - [Phase1.md](./Phase1.md) defines the first execution slice (architecture and security foundations).
   6: - [Phase2.md](./Phase2.md) defines identity, enrollment, and control-plane core delivery.
   7: - [Phase3.md](./Phase3.md) defines Linux data-plane MVP and backend-conformance delivery.
   8: - [Phase4.md](./Phase4.md) defines exit-node, LAN toggle, and Magic DNS delivery.
   9: - [Phase5.md](./Phase5.md) defines observability, reliability hardening, tamper-evident auditability, and early release-integrity delivery.
  10: - [Phase6.md](./Phase6.md) defines admin UX, baseline RBAC/MFA controls, and cross-platform expansion delivery.
  11: - [Phase7.md](./Phase7.md) defines scale and commercial foundation delivery.
  12: - [Phase8.md](./Phase8.md) defines advanced security assurance and compliance delivery.
  13: - [Phase9.md](./Phase9.md) defines completion readiness, long-term operations, and protocol-agility validation.
  14: - [phase10.md](./phase10.md) defines production dataplane enablement for real encrypted exit-node traffic and LAN-toggle enforcement.
  15: - [SecurityMinimumBar.md](./SecurityMinimumBar.md) defines mandatory release-blocking security controls and evidence expectations.
  16: - [MembershipConsensus.md](./MembershipConsensus.md) defines quorum-signed membership governance and tamper-evident membership state verification.
  17: - [MembershipImplementationPlan.md](./MembershipImplementationPlan.md) defines phased implementation work for quorum-signed membership governance.
  18: - If a phase document conflicts with this file, this file takes precedence until requirements are explicitly updated.
  19: - Any new phase capability that changes product behavior must be reflected back into this file.
  20: 
  21: ## 1) Vision
  22: Rustynet is a self-hostable, Rust-first mesh VPN for home servers and homelabs, inspired by Tailscale-style usability while remaining transparent and local-control friendly.
  23: 
  24: Primary goal:
  25: - Securely connect personal devices and home servers into one private network, with optional exit-node routing, optional LAN access through exit nodes, and Magic DNS-like naming.
  26: 
  27: ## 2) Core User Stories
  28: - As a homelab owner, I can join all my devices to one private mesh network.
  29: - As a user, I can select a specific node as an exit node for internet traffic.
  30: - As a user, I can toggle whether I can access the exit node’s local LAN subnets.
  31: - As a user, I can resolve devices by friendly names instead of IP addresses.
  32: - As an admin, I can control who can join, what routes are allowed, and which nodes can be exit nodes.
  33: 
  34: ## 3) Functional Requirements
  35: 
  36: ### 3.1 Identity and Enrollment
  37: - Each device (node) has a stable node identity (public/private keypair).
  38: - Users authenticate to a control plane (self-hosted first; optional hosted later).
  39: - Enrollment methods:
  40: - CLI login flow (device code or auth URL).
  41: - Optional pre-auth keys for headless servers.
  42: - One-time throwaway account/credential generation for temporary access.
  43: - Throwaway accounts must be single-use and become invalid immediately after first successful enrollment.
  44: - Throwaway accounts should support short TTLs, strict scope, and manual revocation before use.
  45: - Node metadata:
  46: - Hostname, OS, tags, owner, last-seen timestamp.
  47: 
  48: ### 3.1.1 Throwaway Account Lifecycle
  49: - `created`: single-use credential is generated with creator identity, scope, TTL, and `max_uses = 1`.
  50: - `used`: first successful enrollment consumes the credential and invalidates it immediately.
  51: - `expired`: TTL reached before use; credential is permanently invalid.
  52: - `revoked`: admin/operator revokes before use; credential is permanently invalid.
  53: - Valid transitions: `created -> used`, `created -> expired`, `created -> revoked`.
  54: - Invalid transitions: no transitions are allowed from `used`, `expired`, or `revoked`.
  55: - Single-use credential consumption must be enforced with atomic write-time revalidation (race-safe, TOCTOU-resistant).
  56: - Credential stores must enforce uniqueness constraints preventing double-consumption under concurrent requests.
  57: - Audit events must be recorded for `created`, `used`, `expired`, and `revoked`.
  58: 
  59: ### 3.2 Mesh Networking
  60: - Node-to-node encrypted tunnels (WireGuard protocol model preferred).
  61: - Automatic peer discovery through control plane.
  62: - NAT traversal using UDP hole punching when possible.
  63: - Relay fallback when direct P2P cannot be established.
  64: - Keepalive and roaming support (IP changes, Wi-Fi to LTE transitions).
  65: - Traversal coordination must use signed, short-lived endpoint hints with anti-replay checks (nonce + freshness bounds) before endpoint mutation.
  66: - Direct and relay path selection must use one deterministic runtime controller (`direct`/`relay` states) with fail-closed outcomes; no parallel legacy/fallback path logic.
  67: - Relay transport is a first-class production capability for hard NAT cases and must forward ciphertext only.
  68: - Runtime must continuously probe relay-backed sessions and automatically fail back to direct when trusted direct connectivity becomes healthy.
  69: 
  70: ### 3.3 Exit Nodes
  71: - Admin can enable/disable exit-node capability per node.
  72: - Client can choose zero or one active exit node at a time.
  73: - Split mode:
  74: - `off`: no exit node (normal local internet).
  75: - `full`: route all internet traffic via exit node.
  76: - Exit node policy constraints:
  77: - Which users/groups can use which exit nodes.
  78: - Optional time-based or tag-based restrictions.
  79: 
  80: ### 3.4 LAN Access Toggle (via Exit Node)
  81: - Per-client toggle: allow/disallow access to exit node local subnets.
  82: - If enabled:
  83: - Client can reach configured RFC1918 subnets behind exit node.
  84: - If disabled:
  85: - Client only gets internet egress through exit node, no LAN reachability.
  86: - Exit node must explicitly advertise allowed LAN routes.
  87: - Route ACLs determine which users may access which LAN subnets.
  88: - Tunnel fail-close behavior must prevent traffic leakage if VPN path drops unexpectedly.
  89: - DNS fail-close behavior must prevent DNS leakage outside Rustynet policy when VPN mode requires protected DNS.
  90: 
  91: ### 3.5 Magic DNS
  92: - Internal DNS zone (example: `*.rustynet`).
  93: - Automatic hostname records for enrolled nodes.
  94: - Optional aliases (e.g., `nas.rustynet` -> specific node).
  95: - Search domain support for clients.
  96: - Conflict handling:
  97: - deterministic naming if duplicate hostnames appear.
  98: - Optional DNS over UDP first; add DoH/DoT later.
  99: 
 100: ### 3.6 ACL and Policy Engine
 101: - Central policy file/API:
 102: - Who can connect to whom.
 103: - Who can use exit nodes.
 104: - Who can access advertised LAN routes.
 105: - Tag-based policy (e.g., `tag:servers`, `tag:family`, `tag:iot`).
 106: - Default deny with explicit allow rules.
 107: - Protocol-specific ACL rules (for example ICMP/UDP/TCP-specific grants) must be preserved and enforced end-to-end, including shared subnet-router and shared-exit contexts.
 108: 
 109: ### 3.7 Administration and UX
 110: - First-class CLI (`rustynet`) for:
 111: - login/logout
 112: - status/peers
 113: - exit-node select
 114: - lan-access toggle
 115: - dns inspect
 116: - route advertise
 117: - Lightweight web admin UI (phase 6) for policy and node management.
 118: 
 119: ### 3.8 Observability
 120: - Node health status (online/offline, relay/direct, latency).
 121: - Connection diagnostics (`rustynet netcheck` style command).
 122: - Audit log for policy changes and auth events.
 123: 
 124: ## 4) Non-Functional Requirements
 125: - Security-first defaults.
 126: - Rust implementation for control plane + client daemon + CLI (as much as possible).
 127: - Minimal external runtime dependencies.
 128: - The WireGuard implementation must be modular and replaceable through a stable backend interface.
 129: - No WireGuard-specific types, config shapes, or assumptions may leak into control-plane APIs or policy schemas.
 130: - A future non-WireGuard backend must be swappable with minimal changes outside backend adapter crates.
 131: - Cross-platform clients:
 132: - Linux (priority), macOS, Windows.
 133: - Setup/runtime host profiling:
 134: - The startup wizard and runtime bootstrap must detect host OS at launch and enforce a host profile (`linux`, `macos`, or unsupported).
 135: - Linux profile may provision dataplane/runtime artifacts and privileged integration.
 136: - Non-Linux profiles must block Linux-only dataplane/runtime operations by default and remain in compatibility mode unless explicitly supported by phase scope.
 137: - Cross-OS runtime artifact segregation:
 138: - Linux runtime roots (`/etc/rustynet`, `/var/lib/rustynet`, `/run/rustynet`, `/var/log/rustynet`) must only be used on Linux hosts.
 139: - On macOS/Windows compatibility hosts, runtime/config artifacts must be stored in user-scoped platform directories and must not create Linux runtime roots.
 140: - Performance budgets (to be benchmarked and enforced in CI):
 141: - Idle daemon CPU target: <= 2% of one core on Raspberry Pi-class hardware.
 142: - Idle daemon memory target: <= 120 MB RSS under normal operating profile.
 143: - Reconnect target after transient network interruption: <= 5 seconds.
 144: - Route/policy update apply target on active clients: <= 2 seconds p95.
 145: - Throughput overhead target versus baseline WireGuard path: <= 15%.
 146: - Benchmarking must run against a documented environment matrix (hardware class, network profile, and OS profile).
 147: - Soak tests for release candidates must run long enough to catch memory/session drift (minimum 24-hour continuous test run).
 148: - Reliability:
 149: - Survive control plane restarts without dropping existing sessions immediately.
 150: 
 151: ## 5) Security Requirements
 152: - Use proven protocols and libraries; no custom cryptographic protocol design.
 153: - Encrypt all node-to-node and node-to-exit traffic with WireGuard-style authenticated encryption.
 154: - Keep the control plane separate and protect it with TLS 1.3 and signed peer maps.
 155: - Use long-lived node identity keys with ephemeral session keys for forward secrecy.
 156: - Support key rotation and rapid revocation/offboarding.
 157: - Relay servers must only forward ciphertext and must not decrypt payload data.
 158: - Store private keys in OS-secure key storage when available; if unavailable, require encrypted-at-rest fallback with strict file permissions, in-memory zeroization, and startup permission checks.
 159: - Treat exit nodes as trusted egress points and rely on end-to-end application encryption (HTTPS/TLS) for internet destinations.
 160: - Enforce authentication attack-surface controls: rate limiting, lockout/backoff controls, and abuse throttling for auth/enrollment endpoints.
 161: - Enforce anti-replay protections for enrollment/auth flows with bounded token lifetime, nonce/state checks, and strict clock-skew policy.
 162: - Enforce web/admin surface protections: CSRF protections, secure cookie/session policy, and clickjacking defenses.
 163: - Enforce API abuse protections (per-identity and per-IP quotas, burst limits, and anomaly alerting).
 164: - Audit logs must be tamper-evident and append-only, with retention rules and forensic integrity verification.
 165: - VPN operating modes requiring protected routing must fail closed for traffic and DNS on tunnel failure.
 166: - Enforce a cryptographic allowlist/denylist policy: reject weak legacy algorithms (for example SHA-1-only integrity, 3DES/BF-CBC-class ciphers, weak DH groups) except behind explicit time-bounded risk acceptance.
 167: - Maintain an algorithm deprecation cadence to remove legacy compatibility debt over time.
 168: - Insecure compatibility modes must be disabled by default; temporary enablement requires explicit, time-bounded risk acceptance and automatic expiry.
 169: - Enrollment key hygiene: one-time credentials default; reusable credentials require strict scope, short expiry, and secret-vault storage policy.
 170: - Require tested vulnerability response workflow with patch SLAs and emergency release capability.
 171: - Require staged release tracks (for example unstable/canary before stable) for security-sensitive changes.
 172: - Patch SLA minimums:
 173: - Critical: mitigation or patched build available within 48 hours.
 174: - High: patched build available within 7 calendar days.
 175: - Medium: patched build available within 30 calendar days.
 176: - Trusted-signing/authorization state must fail closed: when trust state cannot be loaded or persisted, trust-required connectivity must be denied with explicit operator-visible errors.
 177: - Privileged helper and system-integration code must use argv-based exec with strict input validation and must not invoke shell command construction for untrusted values.
 178: - Tunnel/data-path compression for sensitive traffic must be disabled by default to avoid compression side-channel classes.
 179: - Redaction and secret handling requirements apply to all config ingestion paths (MDM, CLI flags, env vars, API payloads, UI forms, and logs).
 180: - Time correctness controls must exist for monotonic-counter dependent handshake logic (clock skew/drift detection and fail-safe handling).
 181: - Traversal endpoint/candidate updates must be authenticated, replay-protected, and freshness-bounded; unsigned or stale traversal hints are rejected fail-closed.
 182: - Direct/relay path transitions must preserve ACL, trust-state, and leak-prevention invariants (no policy bypass during failover/failback).
 183: - Threat considerations:
 184: - Compromised node
 185: - Stolen pre-auth key
 186: - Replay and MITM attempts during bootstrap
 187: 
 188: ## 6) Suggested Architecture (Rust-Centric)
 189: 
 190: ### 6.1 Components
 191: - `rustynet-control`:
 192: - Auth, node registry, policy engine, peer map distribution, DNS records, and signed traversal endpoint-hint distribution.
 193: - `rustynetd`:
 194: - Client daemon handling tunnels, route programming, DNS config, exit-node logic, and deterministic direct/relay traversal path control.
 195: - `rustynet`:
 196: - CLI frontend to daemon + control API.
 197: - `rustynet-relay`:
 198: - Relay/DERP-like ciphertext-forwarding transport for hard NAT cases (deployment may be embedded with control in early environments, but behavior is mandatory).
 199: 
 200: ### 6.2 Data Plane
 201: - WireGuard-compatible transport behavior.
 202: - Prefer direct P2P UDP path.
 203: - Perform authenticated traversal candidate checks for direct path establishment (hole punching).
 204: - Relay path fallback with health probing and automatic failback to direct.
 205: - Reject unsigned/stale traversal endpoint hints before any peer endpoint update.
 206: - Fail closed in protected modes when neither trusted direct nor trusted relay path is available.
 207: 
 208: ### 6.3 Transport Backend Abstraction (Hard Requirement)
 209: - Define a transport backend interface in Rust (e.g., start tunnel, add/remove peer, apply routes, collect stats, shutdown).
 210: - Implement WireGuard as one backend adapter crate, not as globally coupled core logic.
 211: - Core components (`rustynet-control`, `rustynet-policy`, DNS, ACL, identity) must remain protocol-agnostic.
 212: - Backend capability flags must be explicit so alternate backends can degrade gracefully.
 213: - A backend conformance test suite must validate all supported backends against the same networking and policy behaviors.
 214: 
 215: ### 6.4 Control Plane APIs
 216: - gRPC or HTTPS+JSON API for:
 217: - enrollment/auth
 218: - node updates
 219: - peer map fetch/stream
 220: - policy fetch
 221: - DNS record updates
 222: 
 223: ## 7) Roadmap Distribution (10 Phases)
 224: - `Phase 1`: Architecture, crate boundaries, backend abstraction boundary, and security baseline setup.
 225: - `Phase 2`: Identity, enrollment, throwaway credentials, and control-plane core APIs.
 226: - `Phase 3`: Linux data-plane MVP, WireGuard adapter, relay fallback basics, and backend conformance.
 227: - `Phase 4`: Exit nodes, LAN access toggle enforcement, Magic DNS, and CLI feature completion.
 228: - `Phase 5`: Observability, diagnostics, reliability hardening, tamper-evident auditing, and early release-integrity guardrails.
 229: - `Phase 6`: Web admin UX, multi-user workflows, baseline RBAC+MFA controls, and macOS/Windows client expansion.
 230: - `Phase 7`: High-availability scale-out, relay fleet maturity (including traversal coordination and authenticated ciphertext relay transport), commercial controls, and control-plane trust-hardening mode.
 231: - `Phase 8`: Security assurance program, key custody hardening, compliance, and privacy maturity.
 232: - `Phase 9`: Completion readiness, API compatibility guarantees, operational excellence, and long-term protocol agility validation.
 233: - `Phase 10`: Real Linux dataplane enablement for encrypted exit-node traffic, signed traversal endpoint-hint enforcement, deterministic direct-hole-punch/relay fallback behavior, persistent daemon IPC control, NAT/forwarding enforcement, and fail-closed leak prevention validation.
 234: 
 235: ## 8) Phase Planning Rules
 236: - Earlier phases must land the abstractions required by later phases before feature expansion.
 237: - No phase may weaken default-deny policy behavior, key-management controls, or protocol-agnostic backend boundaries.
 238: - WireGuard remains the initial backend implementation, but architecture must remain backend-swappable across all phases.
 239: 
 240: ## 9) Open Decisions to Resolve Early
 241: - Auth model:
 242: - local accounts only vs OIDC first.
 243: - Persistence:
 244: - SQLite for MVP vs Postgres from day one.
 245: - Policy format:
 246: - JSON, YAML, or HCL.
 247: - DNS strategy:
 248: - embedded DNS server only vs OS resolver integrations per platform.
 249: - Relay deployment:
 250: - bundled with control vs dedicated service.
 251: - Licensing:
 252: - permissive OSS vs source-available.
 253: 
 254: ## 10) API / Config Sketch
 255: 
 256: ### 10.1 Node Config Example
 257: ```toml
 258: [node]
 259: name = "mini-pc-1"
 260: tags = ["servers", "exit-capable"]
 261: 
 262: [network]
 263: advertise_routes = ["192.168.1.0/24"]
 264: can_be_exit_node = true
 265: 
 266: [dns]
 267: magic_dns = true
 268: search_domain = "rustynet"
 269: ```
 270: 
 271: ### 10.2 Client Preferences Example
 272: ```toml
 273: [client]
 274: exit_node = "mini-pc-1"
 275: allow_exit_node_lan_access = true
 276: ```
 277: 
 278: ### 10.3 Policy Sketch
 279: ```yaml
 280: groups:
 281:   family:
 282:     - "alice@example.local"
 283:     - "bob@example.local"
 284: 
 285: tags:
 286:   servers:
 287:     owners: ["group:family"]
 288: 
 289: rules:
 290:   - action: allow
 291:     src: ["group:family"]
 292:     dst: ["tag:servers:*"]
 293: 
 294: exit_node_use:
 295:   - users: ["group:family"]
 296:     nodes: ["tag:servers"]
 297: 
 298: lan_route_access:
 299:   - users: ["group:family"]
 300:     routes: ["192.168.1.0/24"]
 301: ```
 302: 
 303: ## 11) Rust Implementation Notes
 304: - Candidate crates:
 305: - `tokio` (async runtime)
 306: - `axum` or `actix-web` (control APIs)
 307: - `tonic` (if gRPC chosen)
 308: - `serde` + `toml`/`serde_yaml` (config/policy parsing)
 309: - `rustls` (TLS)
 310: - `sqlx` (DB)
 311: - Keep unsafe code minimized and isolated.
 312: - Prefer integration tests around networking behaviors and ACL decisions.
 313: 
 314: ## 12) Testing and Validation Requirements
 315: - Unit tests:
 316: - policy evaluation
 317: - DNS naming collision handling
 318: - route/exit-node toggling logic
 319: - Integration tests:
 320: - 2-node and 3-node mesh connection scenarios
 321: - exit node internet routing
 322: - LAN access on/off behavior validation
 323: - relay fallback behavior under blocked UDP
 324: - tunnel fail-close behavior on drop events
 325: - DNS leak prevention behavior under protected-routing modes
 326: - authentication endpoint abuse/rate-limit behavior
 327: - one-time key race/concurrency (TOCTOU) resistance
 328: - protocol-filter enforcement correctness for shared subnet-router and shared-exit contexts
 329: - trusted-state unavailable behavior (must fail closed where trust is required)
 330: - privileged-helper command-input safety tests
 331: - Security tests:
 332: - invalid token rejection
 333: - key revocation propagation
 334: - unauthorized route access attempts
 335: - replay-attempt rejection and CSRF defense validation
 336: - tamper-evident audit log integrity verification
 337: - secret-redaction coverage across all ingestion paths (MDM/env/CLI/API/UI)
 338: - Performance tests:
 339: - daemon idle CPU and memory budget checks
 340: - reconnect latency benchmarks
 341: - policy/route apply latency benchmarks
 342: - throughput overhead benchmarks against baseline
 343: - benchmark matrix coverage checks and 24-hour soak stability checks
 344: 
 345: ## 13) Operational Requirements
 346: - Single binary per component where practical.
 347: - Systemd service files for Linux deployment.
 348: - Startup wizard must enforce OS-aware provisioning:
 349: - Linux hosts: allow full service/dataplane provisioning.
 350: - Non-Linux hosts: block Linux service/dataplane provisioning and emit explicit operator guidance.
 351: - Startup config ingestion must enforce host-storage policy:
 352: - Linux-runtime-root paths found on non-Linux hosts must be rejected or normalized to platform-safe user-scoped paths with explicit warning/audit visibility.
 353: - Structured logging (JSON option).
 354: - Metrics endpoint (Prometheus format preferred).
 355: - Backup/restore strategy for control-plane state.
 356: 
 357: ## 14) Suggested Next Steps
 358: 1. Approve the 9-phase split and lock phase boundaries.
 359: 2. Build execution backlog for Phases 1-3 (foundations, identity/control, Linux data plane).
 360: 3. Define milestone acceptance tests per phase before coding each phase.
 361: 4. Track phase handoff risks explicitly (security, modularity, API coupling).
 362: 5. Run recurring roadmap reviews to keep `Requirements.md` and phase docs synchronized.
 363: 
 364: ## 15) Cross-Document Consistency Rules
 365: - Requirement changes here must trigger updates in [Phase1.md](./Phase1.md), [Phase2.md](./Phase2.md), [Phase3.md](./Phase3.md), [Phase4.md](./Phase4.md), [Phase5.md](./Phase5.md), [Phase6.md](./Phase6.md), [Phase7.md](./Phase7.md), [Phase8.md](./Phase8.md), [Phase9.md](./Phase9.md), or [phase10.md](./phase10.md) where applicable.
 366: - Phase documents may add implementation detail, but may not relax security, ACL, or modular-backend requirements defined here.
 367: - Transport backend abstraction and protocol-agnostic control-plane design are mandatory across all phases.
 368: 
 369: ## 16) Battle-Tested Lessons Applied
 370: - Keep the cryptographic core small, auditable, and protocol-conservative (WireGuard principle).
 371: - Protect handshake/control paths against unauthenticated flood and state-exhaustion attacks with cheap early-drop controls (WireGuard/OpenVPN lesson).
 372: - Treat relays and coordination as untrusted for traffic confidentiality, and preserve end-to-end encryption guarantees (WireGuard/Tailscale principle).
 373: - Enforce strict key lifecycle hygiene (short-lived credentials, revocation, and rotation), especially for automation credentials (Tailscale lesson).
 374: - Enforce explicit policy behavior and test policy changes continuously before release (Tailscale lesson).
 375: - Detect and mitigate routing/DNS leak classes across operating systems (OpenVPN TunnelCrack-era lesson).
 376: - Maintain aggressive patching, security advisories, and staged rollout practices to handle real-world vulnerabilities quickly (OpenVPN operational lesson).
 377: - Keep algorithm policy modern and remove weak/legacy options over time (strongSwan/OpenVPN lesson).

===== /documents/SecurityMinimumBar.md =====

   1: # Rustynet Security Minimum Bar
   2: 
   3: ## 1) Purpose
   4: This document defines non-negotiable security and reliability controls that must be met before release milestones.
   5: 
   6: If this document conflicts with implementation plans, [Requirements.md](./Requirements.md) remains the source of truth and this file should be updated accordingly.
   7: 
   8: ## 2) Release Blocking Rules
   9: - Any unmet `Critical` control blocks release.
  10: - Any unmet `High` control requires explicit, documented risk acceptance by security and engineering owners.
  11: - `Medium` controls may be time-bounded only with a tracked remediation plan.
  12: 
  13: ## 3) Critical Controls (Must Pass)
  14: 1. Proven crypto only:
  15: - No custom cryptographic protocol design in production paths.
  16: - Tunnel encryption uses WireGuard-style authenticated encryption.
  17: 
  18: 2. Control-plane transport security:
  19: - TLS 1.3 enforced for control-plane APIs.
  20: - Signed peer/control data validated by clients before application.
  21: 
  22: 3. Auth and enrollment hardening:
  23: - Per-IP and per-identity rate limiting.
  24: - Lockout/backoff for repeated auth failures.
  25: - Anti-replay protections (nonce/state + short token lifetime + skew policy).
  26: - One-time credential consumption is atomic and race-safe under concurrent requests.
  27: 
  28: 4. Secret and key handling:
  29: - OS key store usage where available.
  30: - Encrypted-at-rest fallback with strict permissions and startup permission checks.
  31: - Sensitive in-memory material handling includes zeroization strategy.
  32: - Trusted authorization/signing state fails closed when unavailable or corrupt.
  33: - Secret redaction verified across MDM, env, CLI, API, and UI ingestion paths.
  34: 
  35: 5. Host-OS boundary enforcement:
  36: - Startup/setup path must detect host OS and enforce host profile behavior.
  37: - Linux-only dataplane/runtime provisioning must be blocked on non-Linux hosts.
  38: - Linux runtime roots (`/etc/rustynet`, `/var/lib/rustynet`, `/run/rustynet`, `/var/log/rustynet`) must not be created/used on non-Linux hosts.
  39: - Non-Linux compatibility mode must enforce platform-safe user-scoped storage paths and reject/normalize unsafe Linux-root paths fail-closed.
  40: 
  41: 6. Policy and privilege enforcement:
  42: - Default-deny ACL behavior across mesh, routes, and exit-node access.
  43: - RBAC enforced on admin API/UI paths.
  44: - MFA required for privileged mutations.
  45: 
  46: 7. Web/admin security:
  47: - CSRF protections for state-changing UI/API flows.
  48: - Secure cookie/session policy.
  49: - Clickjacking defenses.
  50: - Privileged helper/system integration paths use argv-only command invocation with strict input validation.
  51: 
  52: 8. Data-plane leak prevention:
  53: - Tunnel fail-close behavior in protected-routing modes.
  54: - DNS fail-close behavior in protected DNS modes.
  55: - Protocol-filter ACL behavior is validated in shared subnet-router and shared-exit scenarios.
  56: - Direct/relay traversal transitions require authenticated, replay-protected, freshness-bounded endpoint-hint state.
  57: - Path failover/failback cannot bypass ACL, trust-state, or leak-prevention controls.
  58: 
  59: 9. Audit and forensics:
  60: - Tamper-evident, append-only audit logging.
  61: - Retention policy and integrity-verification process active.
  62: 
  63: 10. Supply-chain integrity:
  64: - Signed artifacts required for beta+ releases.
  65: - SBOM generated and retained for released artifacts.
  66: - Staged release tracks (unstable/canary/stable) required for security-sensitive rollout paths.
  67: 
  68: ## 4) High Controls
  69: 1. API abuse detection and anomaly alerting.
  70: 2. Backup/restore validation with integrity checks.
  71: 3. Relay failover tested under fault scenarios.
  72: 4. Tenant-boundary isolation tests (multi-tenant modes).
  73: 5. Incident runbooks and response drills.
  74: 6. Patch SLA tracking and reporting:
  75: - Critical: mitigation or patched build within 48 hours.
  76: - High: patched build within 7 calendar days.
  77: - Medium: patched build within 30 calendar days.
  78: 7. Relay abuse/capacity controls validated under traversal load and reconnect churn.
  79: 
  80: ## 5) Performance Minimum Bar
  81: 1. Idle daemon CPU: <= 2% of one core on Raspberry Pi-class target.
  82: 2. Idle daemon memory: <= 120 MB RSS (normal profile).
  83: 3. Reconnect after transient drop: <= 5 seconds target.
  84: 4. Route/policy apply latency: <= 2 seconds p95 target.
  85: 5. Throughput overhead vs baseline WireGuard path: <= 15% target.
  86: - Benchmark matrix must cover declared hardware/OS/network profiles.
  87: - Release-candidate soak tests must run for at least 24 continuous hours.
  88: 
  89: These budgets are release gates once benchmarking harnesses are active.
  90: 
  91: ## 6) Required Test Evidence
  92: - Unit tests for policy logic, credential lifecycle, and DNS naming behavior.
  93: - Integration tests for mesh, exit-node routing, LAN toggle, and relay fallback.
  94: - Negative tests for auth abuse (rate limits, replay, lockout/backoff).
  95: - Leak tests for tunnel and DNS fail-close behavior.
  96: - Traversal security tests for signed endpoint-hint validation, replay rejection, and failover/failback policy integrity.
  97: - Shared-router/shared-exit protocol-filter ACL tests.
  98: - Audit-log integrity verification tests.
  99: - Performance benchmark report with regression thresholds.
 100: - Concurrent one-time-key consume race tests.
 101: - Privileged-helper command-input safety tests.
 102: - Patch-SLA and emergency-release drill evidence.
 103: 
 104: ## 6.B) Bootstrap Trust Anchor (Membership Owner Public Key)
 105: 
 106: A new node's first contact with the mesh consumes a *signed
 107: membership snapshot*. The owner-signing-key public part is the
 108: trust anchor that lets the node verify subsequent snapshots,
 109: assignment bundles, traversal bundles, and DNS-zone bundles. The
 110: private side never leaves the membership owner's secure keystore.
 111: 
 112: The public side (`membership.owner.key.pub`) MUST reach the
 113: new node *out of band*, before the daemon is allowed to load any
 114: signed state. Every reviewed Rustynet install carries the public
 115: key at:
 116: 
 117: - Linux: `/etc/rustynet/membership.owner.key.pub`
 118: - Windows: `C:\ProgramData\RustyNet\trust\membership.owner.key.pub`
 119: 
 120: Approved out-of-band delivery channels (in decreasing preference):
 121: 
 122: 1. **Pre-baked into the install image.** The reviewed bootstrap
 123:    helper for the install track (e.g. `cloud-init` user-data on
 124:    Linux, MDM device profile on Windows) lays the public key down
 125:    before the daemon's first start. This is the most-secure
 126:    default — the trust anchor is bound to the image build, not
 127:    to any post-deployment trust transfer.
 128: 
 129: 2. **Out-of-band copy from a trusted operator workstation** —
 130:    the operator distributes the public key via SSH or a signed
 131:    file-transfer channel rooted in the operator's existing trust.
 132:    The target host's daemon refuses to start until the file is
 133:    present + ACL'd to root/SYSTEM-only.
 134: 
 135: 3. **Sneakernet / printed thumbprint with pre-distributed
 136:    software.** For air-gapped deployments, the public key is
 137:    printed (or QR-coded) and visually verified against a known
 138:    source. This is rare in normal Rustynet deployments and is the
 139:    fallback for environments that forbid in-band trust transfer.
 140: 
 141: **Forbidden / not approved:**
 142: - Fetching the public key over plaintext HTTP (no trust anchor
 143:   yet, so HTTPS is the *minimum* but the daemon SHOULD prefer
 144:   pre-baking instead).
 145: - Fetching the public key over a TLS-only channel without the
 146:   operator visually verifying the thumbprint — TLS alone does not
 147:   bind the certificate to the membership owner.
 148: - Sharing the public key over a chat channel that does not
 149:   publish key material in a tamper-evident form.
 150: 
 151: **Verification (post-install):**
 152: - `sha256sum /etc/rustynet/membership.owner.key.pub` (Linux) or
 153:   `Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256
 154:   C:\ProgramData\RustyNet\trust\membership.owner.key.pub` (Windows)
 155:   must match the operator's published key thumbprint.
 156: - The file's ACL must be SYSTEM/Administrators / root-only;
 157:   Rustynet's runtime ACL verifier (Linux) and W1.2 verifier
 158:   (Windows) reject non-canonical ACLs at daemon start.
 159: 
 160: This subsection captures the previously-implicit Tofu (trust on
 161: first use) handshake the Rustynet bootstrap performs with the
 162: out-of-band trust anchor; making it explicit closes
 163: SecurityHardeningAudit_2026-04-28.md §B.9.1.
 164: 
 165: ## 7) Phase Mapping
 166: - Phase 1: baseline standards and threat model defined.
 167: - Phase 2: auth/enrollment abuse controls + key custody baseline + atomic one-time key handling.
 168: - Phase 3: encrypted Linux mesh + conformance + initial perf baselines.
 169: - Phase 4: exit/LAN/DNS with fail-close leak prevention.
 170: - Phase 5: tamper-evident audit + early signing/SBOM + perf regression + SLA operations.
 171: - Phase 6: admin UI with RBAC/MFA + CSRF/session/clickjacking + privileged helper hardening.
 172: - Phase 7: HA, tenant boundary hardening, trust-state fail-closed enforcement, and relay/traversal hardening controls.
 173: - Phase 8: external audit cadence + advanced compliance/key custody.
 174: - Phase 9: GA readiness with SLO/DR/performance gates fully enforced.
 175: - Phase 10: real Linux dataplane enforcement for encrypted exit-node traffic, traversal failover/failback integrity, NAT/forwarding hardening, and tunnel/DNS leak-prevention verification in live networking paths.
 176: 
 177: ## 8) Sign-off Checklist
 178: - [ ] Security owner approval
 179: - [ ] Engineering owner approval
 180: - [ ] Operations owner approval
 181: - [ ] Release artifact signing and SBOM verification complete
 182: - [ ] Critical controls all green

 253: ## Executive Summary
 254: 
 255: Rustynet already contains meaningful fail-closed controls around signed state verification, anti-replay watermarks, loopback-only DNS binding, and daemon/helper socket validation. Repo verification showed that some earlier risks were real in code but not wired into the normal install path, and those are now hardened in the current working tree: daemon remote bundle fetch URLs are rejected in hardened daemon paths, bundle staging uses secure create-new local artifacts, privileged helper binary custody is enforced, and remote-ops authorization now rejects same-window replay. Extended read-only passes found additional weaknesses in control-plane enrollment and artifact serialization, relay identity binding and state growth, parser panic handling, phase10 firewall staging, and operator-heavy e2e/reporting paths. The highest-risk remaining gaps are now split between active code and assurance/tooling: supply-chain enforcement is still fail-open in code, enrollment credentials do not appear to constrain enrolled identity, relay session identity is not fully bound to the signed token, the security regression gate has drifted from the actual parser tests, operator-facing privileged orchestration still uses shell-heavy remote execution, and Linux secure-store execution still trusts `PATH`.
