 341: ## 8) Risks and mitigations
 342: 
 343: | Risk | Mitigation |
 344: |---|---|
 345: | VS Build Tools install at `C:\BuildTools` not detected by `Resolve-VsDevCmdPath` | Add explicit fallback path before user-profile lookups; existing detection logic stays as last resort |
 346: | `cargo build` under SYSTEM hits a path that hard-codes `%USERPROFILE%` | Set `CARGO_HOME`/`RUSTUP_HOME` machine-scoped; verify build doesn't write to `C:\Windows\system32\config\systemprofile\` (the SYSTEM profile dir) |
 347: | QEMU/UTM still crashes the guest under load even with GPU accel disabled | Increase RAM to 12 GB; reduce parallel codegen units in `cargo` for the lab build (already controlled by repo `Cargo.toml` profile) |
 348: | Auto-login conflicts with security guidance | Auto-login is to a non-domain local lab account on a developer-only host. Documented as lab-only. Production / live-lab boxes do not auto-login. |
 349: | Inventory or orchestrator behavior diverges between this lab guest and future Windows targets | Keep the orchestrator-side knobs constant. The toolchain-scope decision is a guest-image property, not an orchestrator config. |
 350: 
 351: ## 9) Definition of done
 352: 
 353: - `vm-lab-bootstrap-phase --phase build-release` succeeds against the
 354:   rebuilt guest in under 30 minutes wall clock.
 355: - `--phase install-release`, `--phase restart-runtime`,
 356:   `--phase verify-runtime` each succeed in single attempts.
 357: - `Get-Service RustyNet` on the guest reports `Running` after
 358:   `verify-runtime`.
 359: - Bootstrap report `toolchain_scope` is `"machine"` for all four
 360:   runtime phases.
 361: - No human signed into the desktop during any of the runs.
 362: - `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace
 363:   --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, `cargo test
 364:   --workspace --all-targets --all-features` all pass on the
 365:   bootstrap-script changes.
 366: 
 367: ## 10) Decision log: why option B over A or C
 368: 
 369: **Option A — Auto-login the lab user.**
 370: - Pros: trivial, one `reg` import, works with current bootstrap.
 371: - Cons: requires the desktop to be "displayed" inside Windows (UTM
 372:   console open or kept hot). Closing the UTM window or detaching the
 373:   display can revert `quser` to "no Active session." Fragile in
 374:   headless / CI / multi-VM contexts. Does not remove the underlying
 375:   fragility — if the next bootstrap step also assumes a user profile
 376:   for some reason, we hit the same class of issue.
 377: 
 378: **Option B — Install Rust + VS BT machine-scoped (chosen).**
 379: - Pros: removes the entire "active session" question. UTM can be
 380:   headless. Bootstrap takes the SYSTEM short-circuit path that
 381:   already exists in the script. One-time per image.
 382: - Cons: requires reshaping the resolver functions in the bootstrap
 383:   script. Slightly larger image (machine-scope tools occupy ~3 GB).
 384:   Auto-update of rustup needs to run as SYSTEM (handled by writing
 385:   RUSTUP_HOME to a machine-writable path).
 386: 
 387: **Option C — Pre-baked Windows lab template.**
 388: - Pros: fastest cold-start, deterministic.
 389: - Cons: requires building and storing the template, version-managing
 390:   it, and re-baking on toolchain bumps. Worth doing eventually but is
 391:   a strict superset of B (a baked template still has to install Rust
 392:   + BT machine-scoped). Defer until B is proven.
 393: 
 394: Option B does not preclude option C; once B works the resulting guest
 395: IS a candidate template.

===== /documents/operations/active/WindowsUtmTransportArchitecture_2026-04-30.md =====

   1: # Windows UTM Transport Architecture
   2: 
   3: Date: 2026-04-30
   4: Status: active reference
   5: Owner: Rustynet engineering
   6: Branch baseline: `main` @ work in progress on `awesome-rosalind-5540e1`
   7: 
   8: ## Purpose
   9: 
  10: Document the orchestration transport for Windows local-UTM guests after
  11: the 2026-04-30 rework. Lab orchestration currently uses macOS-hosted UTM
  12: to drive a Windows 11 guest (`Windows.utm`, alias `windows-utm-1`).
  13: 
  14: Two transport channels are available to the orchestrator:
  15: 
  16: 1. **SSH** (`ssh`/`scp` from host to guest TCP/22) — primary for steady
  17:    state, but breaks during mid-orchestration network changes (e.g.
  18:    WireGuard interface coming up, route reordering).
  19: 2. **utmctl exec / utmctl file push / utmctl file pull** — host-to-guest
  20:    over the QEMU/SPICE guest agent, network-independent.
  21: 
  22: The Windows guest needs both because mesh-join changes routing on the
  23: guest side and SSH connections drop. utmctl survives because it never
  24: goes through the network stack of the guest.
  25: 
  26: ## Identity asymmetry
  27: 
  28: The orchestrator's security model and the guest agent's identity disagree
  29: on Windows in a way that does not happen on Linux:
  30: 
  31: | Channel | Identity inside guest |
  32: |---|---|
  33: | SSH (`scp`, `ssh ... powershell.exe ...`) | the SSH login user (`windows`) |
  34: | utmctl exec / file push / file pull | `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` (the QEMU/SPICE guest agent service) |
  35: 
  36: Linux UTM guests do not have this problem because the agent and the SSH
  37: user can be reconciled (root vs. user; `runuser` bridges them).
  38: 
  39: ## Why utmctl previously failed
  40: 
  41: The Windows runtime bootstrap hardens the entire `C:\ProgramData\RustyNet`
  42: tree with `takeown ... /r` followed by `icacls ... /grant:r <user>:(OI)(CI)(F) /T`.
  43: The `/grant:r` flag REPLACES all explicit ACEs, so after bootstrap runs:
  44: 
  45: ```
  46: C:\ProgramData\Rustynet\vm-lab
  47:   WIN-...\windows:(OI)(CI)(F)
  48:   WIN-...\windows:(I)(OI)(CI)(F)
  49:   NT SERVICE\RustyNet:(I)(OI)(CI)(M)
  50: ```
  51: 
  52: SYSTEM is absent. That is the entire root cause of `utmctl file push`
  53: failing with `OSStatus -2700` ("Access is denied" wrapped by an Apple
  54: Events surface). The macOS Privacy & Security Automation permission is
  55: NOT involved.
  56: 
  57: The SSH user `windows` retains access (explicit grant), so SSH/SCP keep
  58: working. utmctl runs as SYSTEM and is denied.
  59: 
  60: ## Architecture: separate orchestration root for UTM-Windows
  61: 
  62: The fix preserves state-tree hardening as-is and instead routes
  63: orchestration scratch to a directory that grants both identities access.
  64: 
  65: ### `utm_staging_dir`
  66: 
  67: A new inventory field carried through to `RemoteTarget`. For Windows
  68: local-UTM targets, it defaults to:
  69: 
  70: ```
  71: C:\Users\<ssh_user>\rustynet-utm-stage
  72: ```
  73: 
  74: That path inherits from the user's profile dir, which by Windows
  75: defaults grants `SYSTEM:F`, `BUILTIN\Administrators:F`, and the user
  76: itself `:F`. Both transports therefore have read+write access. The
  77: state-tree hardening (`takeown C:\ProgramData\Rustynet /r`) does not
  78: reach into `C:\Users\...`, so future hardening cannot regress this path.
  79: 
  80: For non-Windows targets and for future non-UTM Windows targets the field
  81: is `None`; existing `remote_temp_dir` (vm-lab) semantics apply.
  82: 
  83: ### `windows_orchestration_root(target)`
  84: 
  85: Single source of truth. For Windows local-UTM targets, returns
  86: `utm_staging_dir`; otherwise returns `remote_temp_dir`. Used by
  87: `windows_helper_script_remote_path` and
  88: `build_windows_build_release_report_paths`, so every helper script,
  89: result file, and bootstrap report root for a Windows-UTM target lives
  90: under one directory both transports can reach.
  91: 
  92: ### Transport routing for Windows-UTM targets
  93: 
  94: - `run_remote_shell_command_for_target_with_phase` (Windows branch):
  95:   primary path is `execute_utm_remote_powershell_capture` (utmctl exec
  96:   + result file). On utmctl error, falls back to SSH.
  97: - `capture_remote_shell_command_for_target_with_phase` (Windows branch):
  98:   same pattern; output captured via result-file in staging dir.
  99: - `scp_to_remote_for_target_with_phase` (Windows branch): SSH SCP
 100:   directly into the staging dir. Before each SCP, an idempotent
 101:   `utmctl exec` mkdir ensures the staging dir exists (SCP does not
 102:   create intermediate directories). This is network-independent.
 103: - Helper-script invocation in `run_helper_via_local_utm_result_file`:
 104:   SCP helper to staging dir, utmctl exec wrapper that invokes it,
 105:   utmctl file pull of the result file. All three steps share one
 106:   directory; SYSTEM has read access for the invocation, write access
 107:   for the result file, and the host can pull the result file back.
 108: 
 109: ### `execute_utm_remote_powershell_capture`
 110: 
 111: Runs an inline PowerShell script on the guest via `utmctl exec` with
 112: `-EncodedCommand`. Captures the script's output and exit code via two
 113: files written to `utm_staging_dir`, then `utmctl file pull`s them back.
 114: Best-effort cleanup on the way out. The script itself is never
 115: materialized as a file on the guest — it travels in argv via base64
 116: encoding — so identity does not matter for the inner script's source.
 117: 
 118: ## Why this is robust to future state-tree hardening
 119: 
 120: `utm_staging_dir` lives outside `C:\ProgramData\Rustynet`. Any future
 121: tightening of the state tree (additional `takeown /r`, `icacls /T`,
 122: inheritance breaks, group policy) has no effect on the orchestration
 123: channel. Both halves of the staging directory's ACL come from
 124: inheritance off the user profile, which Windows itself owns.
 125: 
 126: The split also prevents accidental re-coupling: when someone modifies
 127: the bootstrap hardening, they do not have to remember "and also re-grant
 128: SYSTEM on vm-lab" because vm-lab is no longer on the orchestration path
 129: for utmctl.
 130: 
 131: ## Field reference
 132: 
 133: - Inventory JSON key: `utm_staging_dir` (string, optional)
 134: - `RemoteTarget.utm_staging_dir: Option<String>`
 135: - `default_utm_staging_dir_for_profile(profile, ssh_user)` — only emits
 136:   `Some` for Windows
 137: - `remote_target_windows_utm_staging_dir(target)` — error if a Windows
 138:   UTM target has no staging dir resolved (either explicit or default)
 139: - `ensure_utm_windows_dir(utm_name, dir, timeout)` — idempotent mkdir
 140:   via utmctl exec PowerShell
 141: - `windows_orchestration_root(target)` — unified scratch root
 142: - `windows_helper_script_remote_path(target, file_name)` — joins via
 143:   the unified root
 144: 
 145: ## Related code
 146: 
 147: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/vm_lab/mod.rs`:
 148:   - `default_utm_staging_dir_for_profile`
 149:   - `remote_target_windows_utm_staging_dir`
 150:   - `windows_orchestration_root`
 151:   - `ensure_utm_windows_dir`
 152:   - `utm_push_to_windows_staging`
 153:   - `build_utm_windows_result_file_wrapper_script`
 154:   - `execute_utm_remote_powershell_capture`
 155:   - `run_remote_shell_command_for_target_with_phase` (Windows branch)
 156:   - `capture_remote_shell_command_for_target_with_phase` (Windows branch)
 157:   - `scp_to_remote_for_target_with_phase` (Windows branch)
 158: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/vm_lab/bootstrap/windows.rs`:
 159:   - `local_utm_result_file_supported_for_phase`
 160:   - `build_windows_build_release_report_paths`
 161:   - `build_windows_diagnostics_invocation`
 162: 
 163: ## Future work
 164: 
 165: - Inline-exec channel for mesh-join stages: even with the staging dir,
 166:   staging files cross the `windows`-user → SYSTEM boundary on every
 167:   call. For stages that run during/after the WireGuard interface
 168:   flips (`distribute_windows_membership`, `distribute_windows_assignment`,
 169:   `distribute_windows_traversal`, `distribute_windows_dns_zone`,
 170:   `validate_windows_mesh_join`), payload can be base64-embedded in the
 171:   utmctl exec argv directly with the result token written to staging
 172:   and read back. This removes the need for any prior SCP, so even if
 173:   SSH is mid-flap the stage completes via utmctl alone. Tracked as the
 174:   next iteration on top of this architecture.
 175: - Eventual lab-LAN Windows targets (no UTM controller) keep using SSH
 176:   with `remote_temp_dir`; no staging-dir changes apply. The
 177:   conditional in `windows_orchestration_root` already handles this.

===== /documents/operations/active/WindowsVmLabAccessOrchestrationRecoveryPlan_2026-04-16.md =====

   1: # Windows VM-Lab Access And Orchestration Recovery Plan
   2: 
   3: ## Objective
   4: 
   5: Close the current Windows VM-lab orchestration gap so Windows UTM guests can be
   6: bootstrapped, reached, and validated authoritatively through the Rustynet
   7: Windows PowerShell path without routing Windows into Linux-only shell stages and
   8: without false-green results.
   9: 
  10: ## Current Status
  11: 
  12: - Windows VM execution is **proven** through local UTM guest exec.
  13: - Windows source sync is **proven** through the current ZIP/PowerShell sync
  14:   path.
  15: - Windows compile capability is **proven** on the live UTM guest by building
  16:   real Rust targets there.
  17: - Windows SSH/access orchestration is **not yet authoritative**.
  18: - Windows bootstrap/install/verify evidence is **not yet authoritative** because
  19:   the access/bootstrap transport and readiness proof remain weaker than the
  20:   guest’s actual execution capability.
  21: 
  22: ## Current Repo Truth To Preserve
  23: 
  24: - `documents/Requirements.md` and `documents/SecurityMinimumBar.md` remain the
  25:   governing source of truth.
  26: - Windows is currently `runtime-host-capable only`, not release-gated and not
  27:   dataplane-capable.
  28: - Linux-only live-lab wrappers remain fail-closed for any target that is not
  29:   `platform=linux` / `remote_shell=posix` / `guest_exec_mode=linux_bash` /
  30:   `service_manager=systemd`.
  31: - Windows helper/system integration stays argv-only and PowerShell-first.
  32: - Windows must not silently reuse Linux runtime roots or Linux shell stages.
  33: 
  34: ## Problem Statement
  35: 
  36: The Windows VM itself is not the primary blocker. The stronger evidence is:
  37: 
  38: - local source sync to the Windows guest works
  39: - guest-side PowerShell execution works
  40: - real Rust code compiled successfully inside the Windows guest
  41: 
  42: The orchestration gap is instead in the Windows access/reachability path:
  43: 
  44: - the access bootstrap helper mutates guest state but does not verify end-state
  45: - local UTM Windows capture still depends too heavily on stdout marker parsing
  46: - Windows local UTM execution falls back to SSH too early, including while SSH
  47:   is still being established
  48: - discovery/readiness collapses distinct Windows failure modes into coarse
  49:   reason codes
  50: - higher Windows bootstrap phases consume those weak lower-level signals
  51: 
  52: ## Scope
  53: 
  54: This plan covers:
  55: 
  56: - Windows access bootstrap hardening
  57: - Windows UTM transport and capture hardening for access/bootstrap operations
  58: - Windows readiness classification improvements
  59: - Windows bootstrap/provider integration for authoritative blocked or passing
  60:   results
  61: - clean-snapshot validation and evidence requirements
  62: 
  63: This plan does not cover:
  64: 
  65: - Windows dataplane/backend implementation beyond the current reviewed
  66:   `windows-unsupported` truth
  67: - release-gate promotion
  68: - Linux live-lab wrapper broadening
  69: - SSH trust weakening or host-key TOFU in the active wrapper path
  70: 
  71: ## Primary Files
  72: 
  73: - `scripts/vm_lab/windows/Enable-WindowsVmLabAccess.ps1`
  74: - `scripts/bootstrap/windows/Bootstrap-RustyNetWindows.ps1`
  75: - `scripts/bootstrap/windows/Collect-RustyNetWindowsDiagnostics.ps1`
  76: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/vm_lab/mod.rs`
  77: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/vm_lab/bootstrap/windows.rs`
  78: 
  79: ## Failure Map
  80: 
  81: ### F1. Access bootstrap returns success too early
  82: 
  83: Current behavior:
  84: 
  85: - installs or starts OpenSSH
  86: - writes `administrators_authorized_keys`
  87: - may create the firewall rule
  88: - returns host-key text
  89: 
  90: Missing proof:
  91: 
  92: - `sshd -t` configuration validation
  93: - deterministic ACL repair/verification
  94: - listener validation
  95: - firewall enabled-state validation
  96: - host-side SSH reachability proof
  97: - structured pass/fail result
  98: 
  99: ### F2. UTM Windows capture is too fragile for authority
 100: 
 101: Current behavior:
 102: 
 103: - PowerShell capture wraps stdout with markers
 104: - CLI parser expects those markers to survive `utmctl exec` output handling
 105: 
 106: Observed failure shape:
 107: 
 108: - `UTM Windows capture output was missing rc marker`
 109: 
 110: ### F3. SSH fallback sequencing is wrong during access establishment
 111: 
 112: Current behavior:
 113: 
 114: - Windows local UTM command failures fall back to SSH
 115: 
 116: Problem:
 117: 
 118: - SSH is the thing being established, so fallback obscures the real failure and
 119:   produces compound error noise instead of a clear root cause
 120: 
 121: ### F4. Windows readiness is under-specified
 122: 
 123: Current behavior:
 124: 
 125: - discovery emits coarse readiness such as `ssh-auth-not-ready`
 126: 
 127: Missing distinction:
 128: 
 129: - host route broken
 130: - guest agent unavailable
 131: - guest IP not authoritative
 132: - firewall closed
 133: - `sshd` not running
 134: - listener missing
 135: - host key missing
 136: - auth rejected
 137: - auth timeout
 138: 
 139: ### F5. Higher Windows phases depend on weak lower-level truth
 140: 
 141: Current behavior:
 142: 
 143: - install/restart/verify depend on helper capture and current transport truth
 144: 
 145: Problem:
 146: 
 147: - if access bootstrap truth is weak, higher-level Windows phase results cannot
 148:   be treated as authoritative
 149: 
 150: ## Phase Plan
 151: 
 152: ### Phase 1. Harden Windows Access Bootstrap
 153: 
 154: **Goal:** make the guest-side access helper verification-based instead of
 155: mutation-only.
 156: 
 157: Files:
 158: 
 159: - `scripts/vm_lab/windows/Enable-WindowsVmLabAccess.ps1`
 160: - `scripts/bootstrap/windows/Bootstrap-RustyNetWindows.ps1`
 161: 
 162: Implementation tasks:
 163: 
 164: - ensure OpenSSH capability installation remains explicit
 165: - ensure `sshd` startup type is correct
 166: - recreate or re-enable the firewall rule when disabled or malformed, not only
 167:   when missing
 168: - rewrite `administrators_authorized_keys` deterministically
 169: - repair SSH file ACLs deterministically using localized administrator/system
 170:   principals
 171: - validate `sshd_config` with `sshd -t`
 172: - restart `sshd` after config/key mutation
 173: - verify the `sshd` service is `Running`
 174: - verify a listener exists on port `22`
 175: - emit structured JSON result instead of only returning the host key
 176: 
 177: Required JSON fields:
 178: 
 179: - `openssh_installed`
 180: - `service_running`
 181: - `firewall_rule_enabled`
 182: - `authorized_keys_applied`
 183: - `host_key_present`
 184: - `listener_ready`
 185: - `default_shell_configured`
 186: - `status`
 187: - `reason`
 188: 
 189: Tests and checks:
 190: 
 191: - PowerShell syntax validation
 192: - unit tests or parser tests on the CLI side for the result schema if the JSON
 193:   contract is parsed there
 194: - negative guest validation for a disabled firewall rule, bad key state, and
 195:   invalid config
 196: 
 197: Phase exit criteria:
 198: 
 199: - guest helper fails closed on invalid SSH config
 200: - guest helper does not report success unless `sshd`, firewall, and listener
 201:   state all validate
 202: - helper output is machine-readable and deterministic
 203: 
 204: ### Phase 2. Split Windows UTM Transport Into Status And Capture Paths
 205: 
 206: **Goal:** stop using fragile stdout-marker capture as the authority for Windows
 207: access/bootstrap bring-up.
 208: 
 209: Files:
 210: 
 211: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/vm_lab/mod.rs`
 212: 
 213: Implementation tasks:
 214: 
 215: - separate Windows local UTM execution into:
 216:   - status/probe path
 217:   - capture-output path
 218: - use exit status or guest-written result files for access/bootstrap probes
 219: - reserve capture-output parsing for workflows that genuinely need payload
 220:   output after transport is already stable
 221: - keep Linux and macOS behavior unchanged
 222: 
 223: Required behavior:
 224: 
 225: - access bootstrap must not depend on stdout markers to prove pass/fail
 226: - access/bootstrap diagnostics must still fail closed if proof cannot be
 227:   retrieved
 228: 
 229: Tests and checks:
 230: 
 231: - unit tests for Windows status-only command execution and parse paths
 232: - negative tests for missing result files or malformed result payloads
 233: - regression tests proving Linux UTM and SSH paths were not weakened
 234: 
 235: Phase exit criteria:
 236: 
 237: - Windows access bootstrap no longer depends on
 238:   `__RUSTYNET_CAPTURE_RC__=...` markers for authority
 239: - result retrieval failures return direct root-cause errors
 240: 
 241: ### Phase 3. Remove Premature SSH Fallback During Windows Access Establishment
 242: 
 243: **Goal:** make Windows access/bootstrap failures report the real broken layer.
 244: 
 245: Files:
 246: 
 247: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/vm_lab/mod.rs`
 248: 
 249: Implementation tasks:
 250: 
 251: - remove SSH fallback for Windows local UTM access-establishment steps
 252: - keep SSH fallback only for operations that are explicitly post-bootstrap and
 253:   already require a healthy SSH transport
 254: - tag Windows transport failures with the exact UTM/probe/readiness cause
 255: 
 256: Tests and checks:
 257: 
 258: - negative tests proving Windows access bootstrap does not attempt SSH fallback
 259:   when the UTM step fails
 260: - regression tests proving non-Windows fallback behavior is preserved where
 261:   currently intended
 262: 
 263: Phase exit criteria:
 264: 
 265: - Windows access bootstrap failure output reports one dominant root cause
 266: - compound `UTM failed; SSH fallback failed` noise is removed from the access
 267:   establishment path
 268: 
 269: ### Phase 4. Add A Real Windows Readiness Ladder
 270: 
 271: **Goal:** make discovery and preflight tell operators exactly what is broken.
 272: 
 273: Files:
 274: 
 275: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/vm_lab/mod.rs`
 276: 
 277: Implementation tasks:
 278: 
 279: - extend Windows readiness and reason-code generation so distinct failure modes
 280:   are preserved
 281: - keep Linux readiness behavior unchanged
 282: - surface the finer-grained reason codes in JSON and user-visible failure
 283:   output
 284: 
 285: Recommended reason codes:
 286: 
 287: - `process-not-ready`
 288: - `guest-agent-not-ready`
 289: - `live-ip-not-authoritative`
 290: - `ssh-service-not-running`
 291: - `ssh-firewall-not-open`
 292: - `ssh-listener-not-ready`
 293: - `ssh-host-key-not-ready`
 294: - `ssh-auth-rejected`
 295: - `ssh-auth-timeout`
 296: - `no-authoritative-ssh-target`
 297: 
 298: Tests and checks:
 299: 
 300: - unit tests for Windows readiness classification
 301: - regression tests proving existing Linux readiness expectations still pass
 302: - report-contract checks for new reason codes in discovery artifacts
 303: 
 304: Phase exit criteria:
 305: 
 306: - discovery reports identify the broken access layer precisely enough to drive
 307:   deterministic remediation
 308: - `ssh-auth-not-ready` is no longer the only Windows access failure summary
 309: 
 310: ### Phase 5. Rewire Higher Windows Bootstrap Phases To Proven Access Truth
 311: 
 312: **Goal:** make `install-release`, `restart-runtime`, and `verify-runtime`
 313: depend on real Windows access/readiness proof.
 314: 
 315: Files:
 316: 
 317: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/vm_lab/bootstrap/windows.rs`
 318: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/vm_lab/mod.rs`
 319: - `scripts/bootstrap/windows/Collect-RustyNetWindowsDiagnostics.ps1`
 320: 
 321: Implementation tasks:
 322: 
 323: - gate higher Windows bootstrap phases on the strengthened readiness/access
 324:   contract
 325: - keep diagnostics collection available on failure
 326: - preserve the current reviewed backend/dataplane truth
 327: - ensure blocked backend cases still return explicit fail-closed reasons
 328: 
 329: Tests and checks:
 330: 
 331: - unit tests for phase gating and blocked-reason reporting
 332: - diagnostics regression tests proving failures still produce a Windows
 333:   diagnostics path when transport truth is available
 334: 
 335: Phase exit criteria:
 336: 
 337: - install/restart/verify consume proven access state instead of weak inferred
 338:   state
 339: - unsupported backend/dataplane truth remains explicit and blocked
 340: 
 341: ### Phase 6. Clean-Snapshot Validation And Proof Refresh
 342: 
 343: **Goal:** prove the new orchestration path on a clean Windows guest instead of a
 344: contaminated troubleshooting state.
 345: 
 346: Operational requirements:
 347: 
 348: - work from a known-clean Windows UTM snapshot
 349: - do not accept stale guest state as fresh proof
 350: - keep host-key trust pinned
 351: - do not weaken Linux-only live-lab guardrails
 352: 
 353: Validation sequence:
 354: 
 355: 1. `ops vm-lab-discover-local-utm`
 356: 2. Windows access bootstrap helper run through the UTM path
 357: 3. host-side pinned SSH readiness proof
 358: 4. `ops vm-lab-bootstrap-phase --phase install-release`
 359: 5. `ops vm-lab-bootstrap-phase --phase restart-runtime`
 360: 6. `ops vm-lab-bootstrap-phase --phase verify-runtime`
 361: 7. diagnostics collection on at least one forced negative case
 362: 
 363: Required artifacts:
 364: 
 365: - dated discovery JSON for the clean snapshot
 366: - dated access-bootstrap result artifact
 367: - host-side SSH proof log or machine-readable result
 368: - install/restart/verify reports
 369: - diagnostics output root for at least one negative case
 370: 
 371: Phase exit criteria:
 372: 
 373: - Windows access is proven from the host, not only from guest-local checks
 374: - install/restart/verify results are authoritative for the current supported
 375:   backend scope
 376: - blocked backend/dataplane cases remain blocked, explicit, and non-green
 377: 
 378: ### Phase 6 Immediate Closure Checklist
 379: 
 380: - patch `scripts/bootstrap/windows/Bootstrap-RustyNetWindows.ps1` so
 381:   `-ResultPath` writes fail-closed JSON on both success and top-level failure
 382: - rebuild `rustynet-cli` after helper-path changes
 383: - rerun `ops vm-lab-start` and confirm Windows access bootstrap no longer
 384:   collapses to `produced no output`
 385: - rerun `ops vm-lab-discover-local-utm` and capture the updated Windows
 386:   readiness artifact
 387: - if access bootstrap still fails, preserve the dominant root cause verbatim and
 388:   do not advance to runtime install/restart/verify
 389: - only resume host-side pinned SSH proof after the access helper result file is
 390:   present and machine-readable
 391: 
 392: ## Milestones
 393: 
 394: ### M1. Verified Windows Access Bootstrap
 395: 
 396: Reached when:
 397: 
 398: - Phase 1 is complete
 399: - the helper emits structured JSON
 400: - success requires real guest-side SSH/firewall/listener proof
 401: 
 402: ### M2. Authoritative Windows Bootstrap Transport
 403: 
 404: Reached when:
 405: 
 406: - Phases 2 and 3 are complete
 407: - access/bootstrap no longer relies on fragile stdout markers for authority
 408: - Windows access bootstrap no longer falls back to SSH while trying to
 409:   establish SSH
 410: 
 411: ### M3. Actionable Windows Readiness Reporting
 412: 
 413: Reached when:
 414: 
 415: - Phase 4 is complete
 416: - discovery and preflight distinguish the real broken layer
 417: 
 418: ### M4. Authoritative Windows Runtime Wiring
 419: 
 420: Reached when:
 421: 
 422: - Phase 5 is complete
 423: - install/restart/verify depend on proven access truth and still fail closed on
 424:   unsupported backend/dataplane cases
 425: 
 426: ### M5. Clean Guest Proof
 427: 
 428: Reached when:
 429: 
 430: - Phase 6 is complete
 431: - a clean Windows UTM snapshot produces dated, repeatable install/restart/verify
 432:   evidence for the current supported scope
 433: 
 434: ## Validation Gates
 435: 
 436: Code-side validation for implementation slices:
 437: 
 438: - `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
 439: - `cargo check -p rustynet-cli`
 440: - `cargo test -p rustynet-cli`
 441: - `cargo clippy -p rustynet-cli --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`
 442: - `cargo check --workspace --all-targets --all-features`
 443: - `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features`
 444: 
 445: Real-environment validation for the orchestration gap:
 446: 
 447: - `rustynet-cli ops vm-lab-discover-local-utm ...`
 448: - Windows access bootstrap through the Windows PowerShell helper path
 449: - host-side pinned SSH probe
 450: - `rustynet-cli ops vm-lab-bootstrap-phase --phase install-release ...`
 451: - `rustynet-cli ops vm-lab-bootstrap-phase --phase restart-runtime ...`
 452: - `rustynet-cli ops vm-lab-bootstrap-phase --phase verify-runtime ...`
 453: 
 454: ## Definition Of Done
 455: 
 456: This plan is complete only when all are true:
 457: 
 458: - Windows access bootstrap is verification-based and machine-readable
 459: - Windows access establishment no longer depends on fragile marker-only capture
 460: - Windows readiness reports the broken layer precisely
 461: - higher Windows bootstrap phases depend on proven access truth
 462: - diagnostics still work on failure where transport is available
 463: - clean-snapshot Windows evidence exists for the currently supported scope
 464: - Windows remains outside Linux-only live-lab shell stages
 465: - unsupported backend/dataplane cases still fail closed and do not produce
 466:   false-green results
 467: 
 468: ## Notes
 469: 
 470: - The Windows VM itself is not the dominant blocker; the orchestration and
 471:   recovery path around it is.
 472: - Do not treat compilation proof or guest-local service/listener checks as a
 473:   substitute for host-side access proof.
 474: - Do not promote Windows support posture based on this plan alone. Docs and
 475:   release gates move only after measured clean-snapshot evidence exists.

  32: 
  33: As of current `main`:
  34:

  36:   path.
  37: - the Windows service/config host is real enough to support smoke validation
  38:   and explicit fail-closed blocker reporting.
  39: - the explicit fail-closed backend label `windows-unsupported` and the opt-in
  40:   reviewed backend label `windows-wireguard-nt` now both exist behind the
  41:   backend abstraction.

  43:   evidenced, not release-gated, and must still be treated as
  44:   `runtime-host-capable only` in support posture.

  46:   must continue to do so.

  59:

  61:   `C:\ProgramData\RustyNet\{config,logs,trust,membership,keys,secrets}` with a
  62:   protected `secrets\key-custody` subtree for OS-secure key custody material
  63: - reviewed Windows runtime passphrase custody now uses DPAPI-protected
  64:   `.dpapi` blobs under the reviewed secret root instead of plaintext long-lived
  65:   runtime passphrase files
  66: - reviewed local privileged IPC is Windows-native named-pipe IPC only, pinned
  67:   to the `\\.\pipe\RustyNet\` namespace with narrow probe and runtime-ACL
  68:   inspection request shapes
  69: - the service installer now repairs reviewed runtime ACLs, provisions the
  70:   reviewed secret roots, and requires an unrestricted service SID
  71: - the Windows verify/diagnostics helpers now capture Windows 11 facts,
  72:   elevation state, service SID state, and the `rustynetd
  73:   windows-runtime-boundary-check` report
  74: - none of this Phase 2/runtime-boundary evidence, and none of the later
  75:   `windows-wireguard-nt` label wiring by itself, is dataplane proof or
  76:   release-gate proof

 118: ## What “Windows Works” Must Mean
 119: 
 120: Windows is only considered genuinely working when all of the following are
 121: true:
 122: 
 123: 1. the Windows service host starts a reviewed runtime path
 124: 2. the backend label is no longer `windows-unsupported`
 125: 3. a reviewed Windows backend exists behind the stable backend abstraction
 126: 4. the Windows node can join a Rustynet network
 127: 5. the Windows node can connect to Linux and/or macOS peers
 128: 6. route behavior is correct and fail-closed
 129: 7. DNS behavior is correct and fail-closed
 130: 8. restart preserves the expected safe state
 131: 9. reinstall from a clean Windows snapshot works
 132: 10. diagnostics and verification scripts collect authoritative evidence
 133: 11. fresh-install evidence exists for the current commit
 134: 12. docs and release gates move only after measured proof exists
 135: 
 136: Until then, service-host smoke proof must stay separate from node-connectivity
 137: proof.
 138: 
 139: ## Remaining Work Streams
 140: 
 141: ### 1. First Real Windows Backend
 142: 
 143: This is the primary blocker.
 144: 
 145: Required outcome:
 146: 
 147: - replace `windows-unsupported` with at least one reviewed backend mode behind
 148:   the existing backend abstraction
 149: - keep backend-specific behavior inside backend adapter code rather than
 150:   leaking it through daemon/domain layers
 151: 
 152: Not acceptable:
 153: 
 154: - using test-only or in-memory behavior as “production” Windows runtime proof
 155: - exposing Windows-looking backend labels that still route to unsupported
 156:   behavior
 157: 
 158: ### 2. Tunnel / Device / Artifact Lifecycle
 159: 
 160: Required outcome:
 161: 
 162: - a real Windows tunnel/device path exists for the selected backend
 163: - artifact presence, architecture fit, and signature state are validated
 164: - create / up / down / remove lifecycle is explicit and repeatable
 165: 
 166: Research carry-forward:
 167: 
 168: - Windows 11 supports the service lifecycle and route/DNS API families needed
 169:   for this work
 170: - Wintun-like artifact validation belongs in the evidence path, not as an
 171:   undocumented manual assumption
 172: 
 173: ### 3. Route And DNS Runtime Truth
 174: 
 175: Required outcome:
 176: 
 177: - route add / readback / remove is correct
 178: - DNS set / readback / remove is correct
 179: - uninstall and rollback do not silently leave stale state behind
 180: 
 181: Security rule:
 182: 
 183: - wrong-state cleanup must fail closed rather than drift silently
 184: 
 185: ### 4. Windows-Safe Local Operations
 186: 
 187: Required outcome:
 188: 
 189: - finish the Windows-safe privileged local IPC path
 190: - finish Windows-safe secret custody and path/ACL enforcement
 191: - keep helper/system integration argv-only and PowerShell-first
 192: 
 193: Security rules preserved from the imported research:
 194: 
 195: - no Unix-socket fallback on Windows
 196: - no remote/UNC pipe use for local privileged IPC
 197: - DPAPI scope should stay narrow by default when service/user scope is enough
 198: 
 199: ### 5. Mixed-Node Validation
 200: 
 201: Required outcome:
 202: 
 203: - Windows node joins a real Rustynet network
 204: - Windows node connects to Linux peer(s)
 205: - Windows node connects to macOS peer(s) when that topology is in scope
 206: - restart and reinstall are proven on current code
 207: 
 208: Evidence classes must stay separate:
 209: 
 210: - host-surface smoke proof
 211: - runtime-boundary proof
 212: - backend functionality proof
 213: - mixed-node proof
 214: - release-gate proof
 215: 
 216: ### 6. Fresh-Install And Release Evidence
 217: 
 218: Required outcome:
 219: 
 220: - clean Windows snapshot or clean guest install proof exists
 221: - current release/fresh-install docs are updated to measured truth only
 222: - required gates run in a proper environment
 223: 
 224: Windows must remain outside the release gate until that proof exists.
 225: 
 226: ## Windows 11 Compatibility Carry-Forward
 227: 
 228: The Downloads-side Windows working bundle contained a useful compatibility and
 229: test matrix. The still-relevant conclusions are preserved here:
 230: 
 231: - Windows 11 is the correct validation target for this work.
 232: - Windows 11 is not itself the blocker; the blocker is the missing reviewed
 233:   backend/dataplane implementation and the evidence burden around it.
 234: - route and DNS API availability are not the main platform concern on Windows
 235:   11; reviewed runtime integration and measured proof are.
 236: - guest architecture, tunnel artifacts, and signature state must be captured in
 237:   every Windows validation run.
 238: 
 239: ## Windows 11 Validation Matrix
 240: 
 241: Capture these on every Windows proof run:
 242: 
 243: - Windows edition, version, and build number
 244: - guest architecture
 245: - UTM guest identifier or snapshot name
 246: - whether the session is elevated/admin
 247: - current Rustynet commit hash
 248: - artifact hashes and signature status
 249: 
 250: ### Phase 1: service/config host
 251: 
 252: Positive checks:
 253: 
 254: - help output advertises `--windows-service`
 255: - help output advertises `--env-file`
 256: - help output advertises `windows-unsupported`
 257: - service image path pins the reviewed binary path and env file
 258: - service start reaches the expected explicit blocker for unsupported backend
 259: - remove/reinstall is repeatable
 260: 
 261: Negative checks:
 262: 
 263: - relative env-file path rejected
 264: - inline daemon flags in service mode rejected
 265: - unknown Windows backend label rejected
 266: - non-reviewed path roots rejected
 267: 
 268: ### Phase 2: runtime boundary and secure local operations
 269: 
 270: Positive checks:
 271: 
 272: - runtime paths stay under reviewed Windows roots
 273: - named-pipe paths stay under the Rustynet namespace
 274: - local-only IPC policy is enforced
 275: - reviewed secret protection round-trip succeeds
 276: - Windows 11, elevation, and service-SID prerequisites are reported explicitly
 277: - diagnostics are sufficient to explain failure without guesswork
 278: 
 279: Negative checks:
 280: 
 281: - Linux runtime roots on Windows rejected
 282: - remote UNC pipe paths rejected
 283: - unauthorized local client identity rejected
 284: - wider-than-necessary secret scope not used by default
 285: 
 286: ### Phase 3: first real backend mode
 287: 
 288: Positive checks:
 289: 
 290: - reviewed backend label parses and dispatches
 291: - required tunnel artifacts exist for the guest architecture
 292: - tunnel artifact signature status is captured
 293: - tunnel create / up / down / remove succeeds
 294: - peer add / update / remove succeeds
 295: - route add / read / remove succeeds
 296: - DNS set / read / remove succeeds
 297: - restart preserves safe runtime behavior
 298: 
 299: Negative checks:
 300: 
 301: - missing tunnel artifacts fail closed
 302: - invalid or unsigned artifact policy fails closed when required
 303: - wrong-state route or DNS cleanup fails closed
 304: - unsupported capability requests return explicit blocker codes
 305: 
 306: ### Phase 4: mixed-node proof and release evidence
 307: 
 308: Positive checks:
 309: 
 310: - clean Windows snapshot install succeeds
 311: - Windows joins a Rustynet network
 312: - Windows connects to Linux peer
 313: - Windows connects to macOS peer when in scope
 314: - restart proof succeeds
 315: - reinstall proof succeeds
 316: - diagnostics and evidence are current-commit and snapshot-clean
 317: 
 318: Negative checks:
 319: 
 320: - wrong backend/runtime state remains blocked
 321: - service/binpath drift is detected
 322: - route/DNS cleanup after uninstall is validated
 323: - stale artifact/signature drift is detected
 324: 
 325: ## Non-Goals
 326: 
 327: This plan does not support:
 328: 
 329: - claiming Windows is already release-ready
 330: - weakening Linux-only live-lab shell-stage guards
 331: - pretending `windows-unsupported` is usable
 332: - moving backend-specific behavior out of the backend boundary
 333: - replacing OS-native protections with ad hoc shell or crypto shortcuts
 334: - promoting helper/bootstrap parity into dataplane/runtime parity
 335: 
 336: ## Definition Of Done
 337: 
 338: This plan closes only when:
 339: 
 340: - Windows is no longer merely `runtime-host-capable only`
 341: - a reviewed backend exists and is proven on Windows
 342: - mixed-node evidence exists
 343: - fresh-install evidence exists
 344: - release docs/gates are updated to measured truth
 345: 
 346: Until then, this document should stay active.

===== /documents/operations/done/ComparativeSecurityFlawAssessment_2026-03-06.md =====

   1: # Comparative Security Flaw Assessment (2026-03-06)
   2: 
   3: ## Scope
   4: - Repository: Rustynet (point-in-time review on 2026-03-06)
   5: - Method:
   6:   - static review of security-sensitive code paths and scripts,
   7:   - comparison against real incidents in similar VPN/network-overlay projects.
   8: - Goal:
   9:   - identify potential flaws (not only confirmed exploits),
  10:   - map external incident lessons to concrete Rustynet hardening actions.
  11: 
  12: Severity scale used:
  13: - `Critical`: can directly enable bypass of trust or tunnel guarantees.
  14: - `High`: materially weakens privileged boundaries or release assurance.
  15: - `Medium`: plausible abuse path, requires chaining or specific conditions.
  16: - `Low`: hardening debt that expands attack surface or future regressions.
  17: 
  18: ## 1) Rustynet Potential Flaw Register
  19: 
  20: ### F-01: Break-glass manual peer programming can bypass signed control workflows
  21: - Severity: `High`
  22: - Evidence:
  23:   - `start.sh:3348`
  24:   - `start.sh:3350`
  25:   - `start.sh:3351`
  26:   - `start.sh:3406`
  27:   - `start.sh:3471`
  28: - Why this matters:
  29:   - Direct `wg set` + `ip route` mutation from interactive shell bypasses centrally signed assignment flow.
  30:   - Compromised admin account or social engineering of an operator can create unauthorized peer/route state.
  31: - Recommended hardening:
  32:   - Remove shell-level manual peer mutation paths and enforce signed assignment workflows as the only mutation path.
  33:   - If a future emergency path is reintroduced, require a signed, short-lived break-glass token and typed validation.
  34:   - Keep explicit audit trail, but make it structured and tamper-evident (signed append records).
  35: - Status: `Mitigated on 2026-03-06 (manual shell mutation path removed)`
  36: 
  37: ### F-02: Peer store input and file-custody controls are weaker than other sensitive state
  38: - Severity: `Medium`
  39: - Evidence:
  40:   - `start.sh:2816`
  41:   - `start.sh:2827`
  42:   - `start.sh:2894`
  43:   - `start.sh:2933`
  44:   - `start.sh:3808`
  45:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/main.rs:486`
  46:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/main.rs:490`
  47:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_peer_store.rs:17`
  48:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_peer_store.rs:30`
  49:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_peer_store.rs:82`
  50:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_peer_store.rs:246`
  51: - Why this matters:
  52:   - Prior implementation relied on shell-managed peer-store validation/read paths, which are harder to reason about and test for strict parsing invariants.
  53:   - Current implementation routes peer-store validation and listing through typed Rust ops commands with custody checks and fail-closed parsing.
  54: - Recommended hardening:
  55:   - Keep strict custody on create/write (`0600`, owner-only, non-symlink regular file only).
  56:   - Keep delimiter/control-character rejection for all persisted peer fields.
  57:   - Preserve one-path policy: `start.sh` must use Rust peer-store ops rather than direct shell file parsing.
  58: - Status: `Mitigated on 2026-03-07 (active peer-store validation/read paths migrated to Rust ops commands; shell parsing path removed from active start.sh peer-store flow)`
  59: 
  60: ### F-03: Privileged helper token policy is broad and not command-schema specific
  61: - Severity: `High`
  62: - Evidence:
  63:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/privileged_helper.rs:454`
  64:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/privileged_helper.rs:481`
  65:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/privileged_helper.rs:486`
  66: - Why this matters:
  67:   - Helper executes high-privilege networking commands.
  68:   - Generic token allow-list still permits punctuation like `;`, `{`, `}`; argv-only execution avoids shell injection, but command-specific parser abuse remains a future risk if callers loosen validation.
  69: - Recommended hardening:
  70:   - Replace generic token checks with per-program/per-subcommand schemas.
  71:   - Reject all punctuation not required by that exact schema.
  72:   - Add negative tests for parser-level argument smuggling.
  73: - Status: `Mitigated on 2026-03-07 (strict per-command nft/ip/wg/etc schemas + negative tests)`
  74: 
  75: ### F-04: E2E remote orchestration shell-execution risk (historical)
  76: - Severity: `Medium`
  77: - Evidence:
  78:   - `scripts/e2e/debian_two_node_clean_install_and_tunnel_test.sh:9`
  79:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/main.rs:517`
  80:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_e2e.rs:789`
  81:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_e2e.rs:2359`
  82:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_e2e.rs:2401`
  83:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_e2e.rs:2412`
  84:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_e2e.rs:2489`
  85:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_e2e.rs:2527`
  86:   - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_e2e.rs:2639`
  87: - Why this matters:
  88:   - Prior implementation used remote shell snippet execution (`bash -se`) for privileged orchestration helpers.
  89:   - Current implementation dispatches all active remote orchestration/probe steps via argv-based SSH command execution helpers and typed Rust ops subcommands.
  90: - Recommended hardening:
  91:   - Keep a single Rust entrypoint (`rustynet ops run-debian-two-node-e2e`) for orchestration.
  92:   - Keep strict token/path validation for all dynamic remote arguments.
  93:   - Preserve test coverage that guards against reintroducing shell payload execution paths.
  94: - Status: `Mitigated on 2026-03-07 (legacy shell orchestrator, remote bash payload scripts, and SSH shell-snippet helpers removed from active path; active orchestration uses argv-only remote command dispatch with typed Rust ops subcommands)`
  95: 
  96: ### F-05: Phase readiness artifacts are validated structurally but not cryptographically
  97: - Severity: `High`
  98: - Evidence:
  99:   - `scripts/ci/check_phase10_readiness.sh:31`
 100:   - `scripts/ci/check_phase10_readiness.sh:40`
 101:   - `scripts/ci/check_phase10_readiness.sh:54`
 102:   - `scripts/ci/check_phase10_readiness.sh:64`
 103: - Why this matters:
 104:   - Gate checks require measured fields and freshness, but do not verify signature/provenance of source artifacts.
 105:   - A forged artifact set can satisfy readiness checks if written to expected paths.
 106: - Recommended hardening:
 107:   - Sign source and derived evidence artifacts.
 108:   - Bind signature metadata to host identity, command digest, and capture time.
 109:   - Fail closed when signature verification is missing or invalid.
 110: - Status: `Mitigated on 2026-03-07 (signed phase10 provenance attestation + fail-closed verification gate)`
 111: 
 112: ### F-06: Some security helper APIs are publicly exposed without current external use
 113: - Severity: `Low`
 114: - Evidence:
 115:   - `crates/rustynet-control/src/admin.rs:97`
 116:   - `crates/rustynet-control/src/admin.rs:202`
 117:   - `crates/rustynet-control/src/admin.rs:216`
 118:   - `crates/rustynet-control/src/admin.rs:260`
 119:   - helper APIs are now test-only (`#[cfg(test)]`) and no longer exported in production builds.
 120: - Why this matters:
 121:   - Unnecessary `pub` surface grows misuse risk and compatibility burden.
 122:   - Makes future hardening/refactoring harder because external use becomes accidental API contract.
 123: - Recommended hardening:
 124:   - Tighten visibility to `pub(crate)` or private for helper-only APIs.
 125:   - Keep exported interfaces minimal and intentional.
 126: - Status: `Mitigated on 2026-03-07 (helper APIs moved to test-only scope; production export surface reduced)`
 127: 
 128: ### F-07: Numeric security configuration is runtime-validated but not type-level constrained
 129: - Severity: `Low`
 130: - Evidence:
 131:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/daemon.rs:205`
 132:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/daemon.rs:216`
 133:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/daemon.rs:217`
 134:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/daemon.rs:218`
 135:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/daemon.rs:221`
 136:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/main.rs:448`
 137:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/main.rs:552`
 138:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/main.rs:564`
 139:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/main.rs:576`
 140:   - `crates/rustynetd/src/main.rs:587`
 141: - Why this matters:
 142:   - Numeric constraints are now mostly encoded at the type level, reducing invalid-value propagation and parser regression risk.
 143:   - Type-level constraints reduce parser mistakes/regressions.
 144: - Recommended hardening:
 145:   - Keep `NonZero*` type constraints for timeout/interval/count fields.
 146:   - Introduce typed CIDR collections instead of `Vec<String>` where feasible.
 147: - Status: `Mitigated on 2026-03-07 (core timeout/interval/count settings use NonZero* and fail-closed SSH allow CIDRs now use typed ManagementCidr values parsed and validated before daemon runtime)`
 148: 
 149: ### F-08: Control-plane signing seed derivation is domain-separated but still custom KDF logic
 150: - Severity: `Medium`
 151: - Evidence:
 152:   - `crates/rustynet-control/src/lib.rs:31`
 153:   - `crates/rustynet-control/src/lib.rs:1512`
 154:   - `crates/rustynet-control/src/lib.rs:2012`
 155:   - `crates/rustynet-control/src/lib.rs:3013`
 156: - Why this matters:
 157:   - Previous approach (`SHA256(domain || secret)`) was deterministic and domain-separated, but bespoke.
 158:   - Migrating to standard HKDF semantics improves cryptographic reviewability and future extensibility.
 159: - Recommended hardening:
 160:   - Replace with HKDF-SHA256 (`salt`, `info/domain`) and versioned derivation labels.
 161:   - Add deterministic test vectors to prevent silent derivation drift.
 162: - Status: `Mitigated on 2026-03-07 (HKDF-SHA256 derivation with fixed salt/info labels + deterministic test vectors)`
 163: 
 164: ## 2) Lessons From Comparable Projects (Attacks + Patches)
 165: 
 166: ### L-01: TunnelCrack (2023) - tunnel bypass across many VPN clients
 167: - What happened:
 168:   - Researchers showed practical tunnel bypass attacks (`LocalNet` and `ServerIP`) affecting many VPN apps.
 169: - How projects patched:
 170:   - Hardened route handling around local network trust and VPN server path exceptions.
 171:   - Reduced client behavior that trusted attacker-controlled local routing context.
 172: - Rustynet lesson:
 173:   - Keep strict route ownership and deny ad-hoc local route exceptions unless cryptographically authorized.
 174: - Source:
 175:   - [TunnelCrack site](https://tunnelcrack.mathyvanhoef.com/)
 176:   - [USENIX paper](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity23/presentation/vanhoef)
 177: 
 178: ### L-02: TunnelVision (CVE-2024-3661) - DHCP option 121 route injection bypass
 179: - What happened:
 180:   - Attackers on local network can push classless routes (DHCP option 121) that bypass VPN traffic.
 181: - How projects patched/mitigated:
 182:   - Moved toward stronger route isolation models.
 183:   - Emphasized namespace-based designs that are less dependent on mutable host routing tables.
 184: - Rustynet lesson:
 185:   - Prefer namespace/interface isolation for fail-closed guarantees.
 186:   - Treat host-route table trust as weak in hostile LANs.
 187: - Source:
 188:   - [Leviathan TunnelVision disclosure](https://www.leviathansecurity.com/blog/tunnelvision)
 189:   - [WireGuard netns guidance](https://www.wireguard.com/netns/)
 190: 
 191: ### L-03: OpenVPN VORACLE - compression side-channel leakage
 192: - What happened:
 193:   - Compression enabled traffic analysis attacks against secret-bearing streams.
 194: - How projects patched:
 195:   - Compression disabled/deprecated in secure defaults and guidance.
 196: - Rustynet lesson:
 197:   - Keep “feature” paths off by default when they weaken confidentiality.
 198:   - Continue explicit prohibition on optional insecure transport features.
 199: - Source:
 200:   - [OpenVPN VORACLE advisory](https://openvpn.net/security-advisory/the-voracle-attack-vulnerability/)
 201: 
 202: ### L-04: OpenVPN Access Server CVE-2025-13086 - malformed request DoS
 203: - What happened:
 204:   - Malformed requests could crash `asd` in some configurations.
 205: - How projects patched:
 206:   - Vendor release with fixed parser/handling (`3.0.2`).
 207: - Rustynet lesson:
 208:   - Keep parser hardening and negative tests for malformed control-plane requests.
 209:   - Treat crashable parser paths as security issues (availability is part of security).
 210: - Source:
 211:   - [OpenVPN Access Server advisory](https://openvpn.net/security-advisory/access-server-security-update-cve-2025-13086/)
 212: 
 213: ### L-05: strongSwan CVE-2022-4967 - authorization bypass via X.509 handling edge case
 214: - What happened:
 215:   - Specific certificate/identity handling could permit impersonation in some setups.
 216: - How projects patched:
 217:   - Fixed in upstream release (`5.9.6`) and documented affected versions.
 218: - Rustynet lesson:
 219:   - Keep identity binding checks strict and explicit in certificate-backed trust flows.
 220:   - Add regression tests for malformed/edge-case identity chains.
 221: - Source:
 222:   - [strongSwan CVE-2022-4967 advisory](https://www.strongswan.org/blog/2023/01/30/strongswan-vulnerability-%28cve-2022-4967%29.html)
 223: 
 224: ### L-06: Tailscale TS-2025-008 - fail-open signer checks when state dir unavailable
 225: - What happened:
 226:   - If state storage was unavailable, signing checks could be bypassed and update checks disabled.
 227: - How projects patched:
 228:   - Fixed startup/update behavior and tightened state handling in subsequent releases.
 229: - Rustynet lesson:
 230:   - Never fail open on missing trust/signing state.
 231:   - Missing security state must produce hard startup failure.
 232: - Source:
 233:   - [Tailscale security bulletins](https://tailscale.com/security-bulletins)
 234: 
 235: ### L-07: Tailscale TS-2026-001 - shell command injection in privileged launch path
 236: - What happened:
 237:   - A local root-command path used `/bin/sh -c` with username templating, enabling command injection.
 238: - How projects patched:
 239:   - Reworked release to remove vulnerable command construction path.
 240: - Rustynet lesson:
 241:   - Reinforces current direction: no shell construction in privileged paths, argv-only execution only.
 242: - Source:
 243:   - [Tailscale security bulletins](https://tailscale.com/security-bulletins)
 244: 
 245: ## 3) Security Hardening Checklist (Prioritized)

 250: - Tighten privileged helper argument validation to per-command schema. (`Completed on 2026-03-07: strict program/subcommand schemas + negative tests`)
 251: 
 252: ### Near-term

 254:

 257: - Upgrade key numeric fields to `NonZero*` types and typed CIDR wrappers. (`Completed on 2026-03-07`)
 258: 
 259: ## 4) Notes on Existing Strengths

 261: - Recent high-value shell-to-Rust security migrations (`F-02`, `F-04`) are now implemented; remaining work is operational validation evidence on Linux VM matrix.

  24: ## Priority 1: Runtime Downgrade Paths (Most Important)
  25: 
  26: ### FL-001: Rust ops failure downgrades to shell implementation
  27: Where:
  28: - `start.sh:578-640` (`ensure_signing_passphrase_material`)
  29: - `start.sh:663-735` (`materialize_signing_passphrase_file`)
  30: - `start.sh:1735-1815` (`prepare_system_directories`)
  31: - `start.sh:2060-2142` (`ensure_membership_files`)
  32: - `start.sh:2152-2182` (`lockdown_blind_exit_local_material`)
  33: - `start.sh:2207-2270` (`refresh_signed_trust_evidence`)
  34: - `start.sh:2458-2475` (`write_daemon_environment` installer path)
  35: - `start.sh:3216-3255` (`set_local_assignment_refresh_exit_node`)
  36: - `start.sh:3371-3415` (`switch_node_role` coupling path)
  37: 
  38: Why it exists:
  39: - Transition period while migrating shell flows to Rust.
  40: 
  41: What can go wrong:
  42: - Rust and shell code paths can diverge in validation, permissions, or failure behavior.
  43: - Attack surface stays larger because shell path remains live.
  44: 
  45: How to make one secure route:
  46: 1. Replace each warning fallback branch with hard failure (`return 1` / `exit 1`) when Rust op fails.
  47: 2. Keep shell code physically present only behind explicit `RUSTYNET_ENABLE_LEGACY_FALLBACK=1` compile-time/profile gating during transition.
  48: 3. Remove legacy shell branches completely after one release cycle.
  49: 
  50: ### FL-002: Secure-delete fallback is best-effort and error-suppressing
  51: Where:
  52: - `start.sh:555-575` (`secure_remove_file_with_scope`)
  53: 
  54: Why it exists:
  55: - Compatibility when `rustynet ops secure-remove` is unavailable.
  56: 
  57: What can go wrong:
  58: - Fallback path suppresses wipe errors (`|| true`), making cleanup failures silent.
  59: - Security guarantees differ by platform/tool availability.
  60: 
  61: How to make one secure route:
  62: 1. Require `rustynet ops secure-remove` success; if it fails, fail closed.
  63: 2. Remove `shred`/truncate shell fallback from production path.
  64: 3. Keep shell cleanup only in dedicated recovery/debug scripts, not normal runtime.
  65: 
  66: ### FL-003: Role/lockdown actions intentionally ignore errors
  67: Where:
  68: - `start.sh:2882` (`lockdown_blind_exit_local_material || true`)
  69: - `start.sh:3927` (same during first-run)
  70: - `start.sh:3392-3406` (role switch post-actions with `|| true`)
  71: 
  72: Why it exists:
  73: - UX continuity during partial failures.
  74: 
  75: What can go wrong:
  76: - Security-critical transitions may partially apply and continue.
  77: - Can leave stale privileged/signing material present.
  78: 
  79: How to make one secure route:
  80: 1. Treat these as transactional operations: any failure aborts role switch/start.
  81: 2. Add explicit rollback if mutation step fails.
  82: 3. Emit a hard error state requiring operator acknowledgment before retry.
  83: 
  84: ### FL-004: Assignment env mutation falls back to inline shell text rewrite
  85: Where:
  86: - `start.sh:3216-3255`
  87: 
  88: Why it exists:
  89: - Backward compatibility if `rustynet ops set-assignment-refresh-exit-node` fails.
  90: 
  91: What can go wrong:
  92: - Shell rewrite path is harder to validate and reason about than typed Rust config mutation.
  93: 
  94: How to make one secure route:
  95: 1. Remove `bash -lc` fallback branch.
  96: 2. Require Rust command success.
  97: 3. Add unit/integration tests around Rust env-file mutation edge cases (duplicate keys, empty values, malformed lines).
  98: 
  99: ### FL-005: WireGuard custody still has compatibility fallback for unsupported binary
 100: Where:
 101: - `start.sh:1924-1935`
 102: 
 103: Why it exists:
 104: - Older installed `rustynet` binaries may not have `ops bootstrap-wireguard-custody`.
 105: 
 106: What can go wrong:
 107: - Behavior can vary by binary version on the same host class.
 108: 
 109: How to make one secure route:
 110: 1. Enforce minimum `rustynet` CLI version before setup starts.
 111: 2. Remove unsupported-command compatibility fallback.
 112: 3. Fail with explicit upgrade instruction instead of running legacy shell path.

 114: ## Priority 2: Crypto / Key-Custody Fallbacks

 116: ### FL-006: OS secure store fallback to encrypted local file
 117: Where:
 118: - `crates/rustynet-crypto/src/lib.rs:350-378`
 119: 
 120: Why it exists:
 121: - Cross-platform operation when OS secure store is unavailable.
 122: 
 123: What can go wrong:
 124: - Local encrypted-file backend is weaker than OS/hardware-backed boundary.
 125: - Inconsistent security posture across platforms/hosts.
 126: 
 127: How to make one secure route:
 128: 1. Introduce strict mode: `require_os_secure_store=true` (no local fallback).
 129: 2. Make strict mode default for production profiles.
 130: 3. Keep fallback only in explicitly non-production profiles.

 133: Where:
 134: - `crates/rustynet-crypto/src/lib.rs:505-515`
 135: 
 136: Why it exists:
 137: - Default flexibility for testing/bring-up.
 138: 
 139: What can go wrong:
 140: - Future callers using `Default` can implicitly permit weaker provider fallback.
 141: 
 142: How to make one secure route:
 143: 1. Change default to `allow_local_fallback: false`.
 144: 2. Require explicit opt-in where local fallback is truly needed.
 145: 3. Add compile-time profile checks to ban local fallback in release builds.

 147: ### FL-008: Explicit emergency macOS passphrase-file fallback toggle

 154: - Emergency recovery escape hatch.
 155: 
 156: What can go wrong:
 157: - Runtime env override can re-enable file passphrase path.
 158: 
 159: How to make one secure route:
 160: 1. Remove runtime env toggle in production build/profile.
 161: 2. Keep recovery behavior in a separate offline recovery binary/tool.
 162: 3. Add startup gate that hard-fails if this env var is set in production mode.

 165: Where:

 168: Why it exists:
 169: - Shared implementation naming from earlier custody design.
 170: 
 171: What can go wrong:
 172: - Naming and API surface encourage ongoing fallback semantics.

 174: How to make one secure route:
 175: 1. Rename to neutral mandatory API (`encrypt_private_key_envelope`), or move behind internal module.

 267: ### FL-015: Dependency installer fallback for ripgrep via cargo
 268: Where:
 269: - `start.sh:1383-1397`

 271: Why it exists:

 273: 
 274: What can go wrong:
 275: - Non-uniform toolchain/provenance across systems.
 276: 
 277: How to make one secure route:
 278: 1. Require one package manager path per platform.
 279: 2. Fail with installation instructions rather than alternate installer logic.
 280: 
 281: ## Priority 1 (Addendum): Additional Runtime Downgrade Paths
 282: 
 283: ### FL-016: macOS runtime path coercion still relies on compatibility namespace defaults
 284: Where:
 285: - `start.sh:117-137` (`apply_host_profile_defaults`)
 286: - `start.sh:153-166` (`coerce_macos_path_var`)
 287: - `start.sh:219-237` (`enforce_host_storage_policy`)
 288: 
 289: Why it exists:
 290: - Keep older path conventions and mixed host-profile configs working during migration.
 291: 
 292: What can go wrong:
 293: - Silent path rewrites hide config drift instead of forcing explicit correction.
 294: - `compat/...` namespace keeps legacy assumptions alive for trust/assignment/key paths.
 295: 
 296: How to make one secure route:
 297: 1. Define one canonical macOS path set without `compat/` aliases.
 298: 2. Move coercion to a one-time migration command that writes canonical values.
 299: 3. Fail startup when non-canonical storage paths are detected after migration.
 300: 
 301: ### FL-017: Pre-start trust refresh failure is warn-only when auto-refresh is enabled
 302: Where:
 303: - `start.sh:2885-2887`
 304: 
 305: Why it exists:
 306: - Preserve startup continuity during transient signer/refresh failures.
 307: 
 308: What can go wrong:
 309: - Service can start with stale trust evidence even when refresh is explicitly enabled.
 310: - Startup security behavior differs between “refresh succeeded” and “refresh failed but continued” states.
 311: 
 312: How to make one secure route:
 313: 1. If `AUTO_REFRESH_TRUST=1` and signer material is present, require successful refresh before daemon start.
 314: 2. On refresh failure, abort startup with explicit remediation guidance.
 315: 3. Keep a separate explicit break-glass command for emergency manual starts (audited, time-bounded).
 316: 
 317: ### FL-018: Temporary signing-passphrase file ownership/mode hardening suppresses errors
 318: Where:
 319: - `start.sh:675-677`
 320: - `start.sh:692-693`
 321: - `start.sh:713-714`
 322: 
 323: Why it exists:
 324: - Tolerate chown/chmod quirks across privilege boundaries in mixed setups.
 325: 
 326: What can go wrong:
 327: - Temporary passphrase files may remain with incorrect owner/mode without failing the operation.
 328: - Security guarantees depend on ambient filesystem defaults instead of enforced custody.
 329: 
 330: How to make one secure route:
 331: 1. Treat `chown`/`chmod` failures as hard errors.
 332: 2. Secure-remove temp files immediately on permission-hardening failure.
 333: 3. Prefer Rust-side materialization that atomically creates the temp file with final owner/mode.
 334: 
 335: ### FL-019: VPN disconnect teardown is mostly best-effort and can leave residual dataplane state
 336: Where:
 337: - `start.sh:2923-2935` (macOS helper/PF cleanup ignores failures)
 338: - `start.sh:2954-2993` (Linux route/rule/nft/sysctl cleanup is warn-only)
 339: 
 340: Why it exists:
 341: - Prioritize user recoverability even when some teardown steps fail.
 342: 
 343: What can go wrong:
 344: - Residual routing/firewall state can persist across reconnects and role changes.
 345: - Hard-to-diagnose stale network state increases operational and security risk.
 346: 
 347: How to make one secure route:
 348: 1. Replace shell teardown with one Rust “disconnect/cleanup” op that returns structured residual-state errors.
 349: 2. Fail disconnect when critical cleanup steps do not complete.
 350: 3. Offer a separate explicit `ops recover-network` command for forced remediation paths.
 351: 
 352: ## Priority 2 (Addendum): Additional Crypto / Key-Custody Fallbacks
 353: 
 354: ### FL-020: Systemd installer has a separate weaker secure-remove implementation
 355: Where:
 356: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/ops_install_systemd.rs:1411-1447`
 357: 
 358: Why it exists:
 359: - Historical local utility implementation inside installer module.
 360: 
 361: What can go wrong:
 362: - Behavior diverges from stricter secure-remove logic used elsewhere.
 363: - Non-regular file targets return success (`Ok(())`) without explicit operator visibility.
 364: 
 365: How to make one secure route:
 366: 1. Consolidate all secure-delete calls onto one shared Rust implementation.
 367: 2. Return explicit errors for unsupported file types (except not-found).
 368: 3. Require fsync + truncation/wipe semantics consistency across all call sites.
 369: 
 370: ### FL-021: Daemon key-material deletion uses best-effort scrub with suppressed write errors
 371: Where:
 372: - `crates/rustynetd/src/key_material.rs:516-548`
 373: 
 374: Why it exists:
 375: - Avoid blocking deletion when overwrite/sync operations are partially unavailable.
 376: 
 377: What can go wrong:
 378: - Scrub write/sync failures are not surfaced, so wipe guarantees are unverifiable.
 379: - Sensitive file deletion can silently degrade to plain remove behavior.
 380: 
 381: How to make one secure route:
 382: 1. Convert best-effort scrub to strict scrub that returns errors.
 383: 2. Propagate failures to callers for revoke/cleanup operations.
 384: 3. Add tests that assert failure on scrub I/O errors rather than silent continuation.
 385: 
 386: ### FL-022: Denylisted algorithm handling includes compatibility-exception bypass path
 387: Where:
 388: - `crates/rustynet-crypto/src/lib.rs:149-167`
 389: - `crates/rustynet-crypto/src/lib.rs:179-189`
 390: 
 391: Why it exists:
 392: - Controlled temporary compatibility path for denylisted algorithms.
 393: 
 394: What can go wrong:
 395: - A denylisted algorithm can be accepted through exception wiring, which preserves a downgrade route.
 396: - Exception model is expiry-based at this layer and does not itself enforce richer signed risk context.
 397: 
 398: How to make one secure route:
 399: 1. Remove runtime algorithm exceptions in production profile.
 400: 2. If exceptions must exist, require signed risk-acceptance payloads and enforce them at the validation boundary.
 401: 3. Add gate checks that fail production builds when exception list is non-empty.
 402: 
 403: ## Priority 4 (Addendum): Additional Operational Compatibility Fallbacks
 404: 
 405: ### FL-023: CI security-gate toolchain resolution falls back to ambient cargo toolchain
 406: Where:
 407: - `scripts/ci/phase1_gates.sh:81-87`, `94-97`
 408: - `scripts/ci/phase10_gates.sh:81-87`, `94-97`
 409: - `scripts/ci/membership_gates.sh:81-87`, `94-97`
 410: 
 411: Why it exists:
 412: - Keep gates runnable when pinned security toolchain is unavailable.
 413: 
 414: What can go wrong:
 415: - Security scan behavior varies by environment/toolchain availability.
 416: - Gate outcomes become less deterministic across hosts.
 417: 
 418: How to make one secure route:
 419: 1. Require one pinned security toolchain and fail if unavailable.
 420: 2. Require one deterministic advisory-db source path (pre-synced artifact).
 421: 3. Remove fallback branch that runs `cargo` without the pinned toolchain.
 422: 
 423: ### FL-024: Dependency/bootstrap flows still include compatibility install branches with dynamic remote installers
 424: Where:
 425: - `start.sh:1083` (Homebrew installer via remote script)
 426: - `start.sh:1187-1199` (cargo-deny compatibility version branch)
 427: - `start.sh:1208` (rustup bootstrap via remote script)
 428: 
 429: Why it exists:
 430: - Simplify first-run bootstrap across diverse host states.
 431: 
 432: What can go wrong:
 433: - Multiple bootstrap paths increase provenance and reproducibility variance.
 434: - Security posture depends on live network installer behavior.
 435: 
 436: How to make one secure route:
 437: 1. Use a single package/bootstrap route per platform with pinned versions/checksums.
 438: 2. Fail setup when required toolchain packages are not present from approved source.
 439: 3. Keep remote-script bootstrap as documented manual break-glass only.
 440: 
 441: Update 2026-03-07:
 442: - Operator/bootstrap flow in `start.sh` now uses host package-manager `rustup` plus the pinned workspace toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml`; ambient distro `cargo`/`rustc` fallback is removed from that path.
 443: - Remote E2E host bootstrap (`rustynet ops e2e-bootstrap-host`) now enforces the pinned repo toolchain when it performs its own build and skips the redundant privileged rebuild path when the caller already installed the binaries.
 444: - Assignment refresh env writers now emit quoted env-file assignments for structured values (`RUSTYNET_ASSIGNMENT_NODES`, `RUSTYNET_ASSIGNMENT_ALLOW`, and related fields), closing the raw-shell metacharacter parsing path in both systemd `EnvironmentFile` consumption and shell-sourced E2E harnesses.
 445: - Signing passphrase materialization now decrypts into a fresh secure temp directory path and atomically publishes the requested output; the ad hoc direct decrypt-to-existing-file pattern is removed from the live E2E matrix path.
 446: - CI helper script `scripts/ci/bootstrap_ci_tools.sh` still needs separate remediation before FL-024 can be considered fully closed repository-wide.
 447: 
 448: ### FL-025: macOS launchd bootout helper suppresses unload errors
 449: Where:
 450: - `start.sh:2631-2643`
 451: - Called by: `start.sh:2849-2850`, `2871-2872`
 452: 
 453: Why it exists:
 454: - Tolerate differences in launchd bootout syntax and unit state.
 455: 
 456: What can go wrong:
 457: - Stale launchd units can persist without visibility when both bootout forms fail.
 458: - Subsequent bootstrap may run against partially stale service state.
 459: 
 460: How to make one secure route:
 461: 1. Keep dual-syntax attempt if needed, but require one explicit success condition.
 462: 2. If both attempts fail, fail the operation with actionable diagnostics.
 463: 3. Add explicit post-check (`launchctl print`) to verify unit unload state.
 464: 
 465: ### FL-026: Invalid persisted config values are silently coerced to defaults
 466: Where:
 467: - `start.sh:277-284` (invalid/unsupported `NODE_ROLE` -> `client`)
 468: - `start.sh:788-821` (invalid `EXIT_CHAIN_HOPS`/launch defaults reverted)
 469: 
 470: Why it exists:
 471: - Keep startup/menu flow resilient when config contents are malformed.
 472: 
 473: What can go wrong:
 474: - Misconfiguration or tampering can be masked by silent coercion.
 475: - Operators may not realize runtime posture changed from intended configuration.
 476: 
 477: How to make one secure route:
 478: 1. Treat invalid persisted security-relevant config as startup error, not auto-rewrite.
 479: 2. Provide explicit `ops repair-config` command that validates and rewrites values with operator confirmation.
 480: 3. Persist only validated config schema versions and reject unknown/invalid fields.
 481: 
 482: ### FL-027: Network/backend parameters are coerced to safe defaults instead of requiring explicit correction
 483: Where:
 484: - `start.sh:240-243` (invalid macOS `WG_INTERFACE` -> `utun9`)
 485: - `start.sh:448-457` (unsupported backend forced to host expected backend)
 486: - `start.sh:479-483` (invalid WireGuard listen port -> `51820`)
 487: 
 488: Why it exists:
 489: - Improve setup survivability across partial or stale configurations.
 490: 
 491: What can go wrong:
 492: - Runtime may proceed with unintended interface/backend/port values.
 493: - Silent coercion can hide deployment drift and complicate incident response.
 494: 
 495: How to make one secure route:
 496: 1. Fail on invalid backend/interface/port with explicit remediation output.
 497: 2. Keep defaults only for initial provisioning, never for previously persisted configs.
 498: 3. Add startup integrity check that blocks run when persisted values are out of policy.
 499: 
 500: ### FL-028: Trust/assignment publication group selection falls back to root group when daemon group is missing
 501: Where:
 502: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/main.rs:3295-3301` (`group_gid_or_root`)
 503: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/main.rs:1227-1233` (trust refresh publication mode selection)
 504: - `crates/rustynet-cli/src/main.rs:1353-1368` (assignment refresh directory ownership)
 505: 
 506: Why it exists:
 507: - Keep refresh operations running on hosts where daemon group bootstrap is incomplete.
 508: 
 509: What can go wrong:
 510: - Group-custody intent is silently downgraded to root-group ownership.
 511: - Permission profile changes depend on host bootstrap state instead of explicit policy.
 512: 
 513: How to make one secure route:
 514: 1. Remove root-group fallback and require daemon group existence before refresh/install operations.
 515: 2. Fail with explicit remediation (`ops install-systemd` / group bootstrap) when missing.
 516: 3. Add test coverage asserting no implicit group fallback for trust/assignment artifact ownership.
 517: 
 518: ## Execution Order To Remove Fallbacks Safely
 519: 
 520: 1. Remove Priority 1 items (`FL-001` through `FL-005`) and enforce fail-closed runtime behavior.
 521: 2. Apply strict custody/provider policy (`FL-006` through `FL-009`) with production profile gates.
 522: 3. Migrate and drop legacy format/path acceptance (`FL-010`, `FL-011`).
 523: 4. Remove addendum runtime/custody downgrade paths (`FL-016` through `FL-022`).
 524: 5. Harden operational determinism and CI/bootstrap consistency (`FL-012` through `FL-015`, `FL-023` through `FL-028`).
